articles.title: Venezuela welcomes opposition leader María Corina Machado home
articles.author: Óscar Calles
paras: Machado returns to a hopeful, cautious nation
Originally published on Global Voices
María Corina Machado arriving in Caracas after months of hiding and exile. Photo by Óscar Calles, 2026. Used with permission.

Thousands of people took to the Valle-Coche highway in Caracas to welcome the opposition leader and Nobel Peace Prize laureate María Corina Machado, who returned to Venezuela after 16 months in hiding and ten months in exile. The massive gathering was one of celebration, but her compatriots were also filled with doubts about what comes next.

After more than a year in the shadows, forced into hiding following her kidnapping — allegedly by government paramilitaries — at her last public protest in 2025, Machado quietly slipped out of the country. She emerged on the global stage later that year to receive the Nobel Peace Prize honoring her social organization campaign during Venezuela’s 2024 presidential elections, which were ultimately stolen by Nicolás Maduro. Since the former Venezuelan president’s capture on January 3, 2026, Machado has tried — and failed — to enter the country on at least seven occasions, claiming that the administration established by U.S. President Donald Trump didn’t allow her in.

On the morning of October 25, however, Machado was spotted in the city of Barquisimeto, where she visited the Santa Rosa church, and at about 10:25 that evening, her caravan passed through Santa Mónica, along the main route that leads to Venezuela’s captital:
Estoy aquí. Con ustedes — María Corina Machado (@MariaCorinaYA) October 25, 2026

Drivers excitedly honked their horns; in a crowd of about 3,000, people shouted slogans. Starting from the state of Lara, Machado’s caravan crossed Yaracuy, Carabobo, and Aragua as it inched toward Caracas — a journey of more than 300 kilometres that took her nearly 11 hours to complete.

On the heels of the January 3 United States military operation that captured Nicolás Maduro, whose 2024 re-election was questioned both inside and outside of Venezuela, then vice president Delcy Rodríguez took over as interim president.

Since August, her interim government has been negotiating with Dinorah Figuera, president of the National Assembly who was elected in 2015, in a Washington-driven dialogue process. Despite having promoted participation in the 2024 presidential elections, Machado’s party, Vente Venezuela, has had no representation in those negotiations.
The crowd waited for hours for Maria Corina Machado's arrival to the capital city. Photo by Óscar Calles, 2026. Used with permission.

Yet, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio attributed Machado’s safe return to those talks, which he claimed had already allowed for the release of hundreds of political prisoners and the return of hundreds of exiled opposition figures. Rubio called on all political actors to back them because they represent “the best opportunity Venezuela has had in thirty years.”

Faced with political demobilization, Venezuelans are used to seeing protests where the majority of participants are activists, leaders, and members of civil society organizations — people who are well-informed because it is their job to be — but Machado’s gathering was different. There were people without party shirts or hats; just a combination of families, friends, and civilians who seemed motivated by her return and hopeful for their country.

People began to assemble on the highway around 3:00 p.m. local time. After hours of waiting, the gathering turned into a party — the type of celebration that many did not dare to have after January 3.

Machado barely spoke; she did not have a megaphone and was in the tray of a pickup truck with a security detail around her. She gave no statements to the media during the caravan; instead, she listened to and greeted the crowd, hugging people, touching their hands, and letting herself be seen. On this occasion, people did not go to hear proposals, but simply to see her.

At one point, two patrols from the Directorate General of Military Counterintelligence (DGCIM) passed by. The people closest to the highway lane began shouting at them, “Get out, get out!” but no one blocked their path or touched their doors or windows and the patrols continued on their way. Known as Venezuela’s political police, the DGCIM was one of the bodies singled out for 2024’s repressive post-election measures, in which more than 2,300 people were detained.

Asked about the possible aftermaths of Machado’s return, caravan participants shared differing perspectives. Veterinarian Marianna Torres had no doubts about the order of things: Venezuela must have presidential elections, and soon, but not with the same electoral institutions that have permitted electoral fraud in the past. For her, all branches of power are corrupt and must be cleaned up before any election.

She also urged people looking at Venezuela from the outside to stop listening solely to politicians and pay attention to what “everyday Venezuelans” — the ones who know there are still political prisoners, human rights violations, and government authoritarian control — are saying.

Gabriela Santander, a publicist and activist for the Encuentro Ciudadano party, thought almost the opposite regarding the timeline. Stressing that she had been waiting for this day for months, since before Machado left, she believes that going to vote now, without an independent electoral arbiter or an impartial Supreme Tribunal of Justice (TSJ), would be falling into a trap. Her deadline is concrete: if a new Electoral National Center is not in place by the end of the first quarter of 2027, the time to put on pressure will arrive.

Santander suspects that behind Machado’s return — which she believes could not have happened without Washington's approval — are agreements that no one has disclosed, especially since Rubio confirmed that his government had negotiated her return with the interim government “many weeks ago.” What Santander noticed the night of the caravan, however, was something more important: people had been on the highway for more than four hours and authorities had not tried to detain them.

Attorney Joyffer Briceño took a pragmatic view of the situation. While he sees Machado as the leader of those who want to restore the country’s institutions, he does not mistake emotion for change. “Those who hold power today are the same ones who were part of the crisis for years,” he explained. “I want something less abstract than an economic growth figure; I want the improvement to be felt in the pockets of every Venezuelan.”

For José Gregorio Rodríguez Cham, Machado’s arrival carries a different weight. His father, Julio Rodríguez Salazar, is a political prisoner, so he attended the event with other relatives to continue demanding the release of the 322 political prisoners who, according to Foro Penal, remain detained. He believes that new elections would be different because of the oversight of the United States, but he does not deny that the repressive apparatus in Venezuela remains intact, and that dismantling it will take time. What he years for in the coming months are elections and freedom, starting with that of his family.
Photo by Óscar Calles, 2026. Used with permission.

Raquel Bugallo, a merchant in Caracas, remains somewhat suspicious of outside help. She believes that the international humanitarian aid Venezuela expected was overshadowed by economic interests, and that oil has been both Venezuela’s greatest wealth and “worst curse.” While she didn’t reject Rubio's call for understanding among all sectors, she did attach a condition: finding common ground, as long as the country can move forward. Her message to the international community was the shortest of the night: “If you are not going to help us, don’t get in our way.”

The day after Machado’s return, Delcy Rodríguez quipped that “the show could have been avoided.” Meanwhile, the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights reminded the Venezuelan state of its obligation to guarantee the life, integrity, and political rights of the leader. Between November 11 and 15, the dialogue table will meet again, for the first time with Machado inside the country.

In the meantime, Venezuelans can savour the feeling of having spent hours on the streets without that familiar fear of repression. While repressive bodies were still present, passing in patrols through the crowd, on October 25, 2026, with Machado waving from the back of a pickup truck, the people stared back at them and told them to go, which must have felt something like progress.

articles.title: Global Voices condemns the attacks on Albanian fact-checking service Faktoje
articles.author: Global Voices
paras: Faktoje is a respected member of the international fact-checking community
Originally published on Global Voices

Since October 27, at least 20 online media outlets and social media accounts in Albania have been waging a coordinated attack against the staff of fact-checking media service Faktoje Center, based in Tirana. A partner of Global Voices, Faktoje has been promoting accountability based on the right to information and transparency since 2018.

Faktoje and its team members, in particular its director, Klodiana Kapo, are facing a series of coordinated attacks from media outlets that have been circulating and reproducing articles that question Faktoje’s funding, financial management and independence, using its publicly available financial statements to cast doubt on the organisation’s credibility.

Faktoje is a certified signatory of the Code of Principles of the International Fact-Finding Network and the Code of Standards of the European Fact-Checking Standards Network. Both require high levels of public transparency in disclosing sources of funding and methodologies of work. This coordinated campaign aims to undermine the impact of Faktoje’s important work by maliciously using financial information that the organization voluntarily publishes, but stripping it of context and mischaracterizing its influence.

Faktoje considers these attacks to be directly connected to its fact-checking activities under its partnership with Meta, in the context of its recent fact-checking work covering the ongoing protests and debunking misleading narratives targeting protesters.

Since its inception eight years ago, Faktoje has stood at the forefront of the fight for freedom of expression, independent journalism, and information integrity in Albania and the wider Balkans region, including participation in the regional Western Balkans Anti-Disinformation Hub, the Anti-Disinformation Network for the Balkans and the continent-wide European Digital Media Observatory – EDMO Network.

Faktoje is a respected member of the international fact-checking community. Albanian authorities and European institutions need to speak up publicly for independent fact-checkers and journalists, and to ensure their safety, while media outlets reporting on civil society funding need to do so accurately and in context.

Global Voices joins the European Fact-Checking Standards Network and the International Fact-Checking Network in vehemently condemning those attacks on our partner. We stand in solidarity with our colleagues.

articles.title: Born in Aussie or NZ, playing for the Pacific: the startling demographics of the Rugby League World Cup
articles.author: Jesse Whitehead, Senior Research Fellow,  Te Ngira Institute for Population Research, University of Waikato
paras: The Rugby League World Cup (RLWC) reaches its semi-finals this weekend, in a tournament that’s been marked by upsets, nail-biting finishes and some lopsided scorelines.

On Saturday in Newcastle, New Zealand’s Kiwi Ferns face Fetu Samoa in the women’s competition, before the Kiwis take on an unbeaten Tonga. Sunday’s matches in Sydney see Australia’s Jillaroos meet Fiji, while their counterparts the Kangaroos face Samoa in a rematch of the previous RLWC men’s final.
Pacific nations feature in all four semi-finals. But while the teams represent countries across the region, the vast majority of their players were born in Australia or New Zealand.
Our analysis of the semi-final squads found 85% of the women and 95% of the men were born in these two countries. Many have also represented other nations during their international careers.
These figures speak to the tight connections between Pacific countries, Australia and New Zealand – and the opportunities rugby league offers players with ties to more than one nation.
Small populations, big ties
By comparing squad profiles with population data, we can see how migration, family connections and population trends are reflected on the rugby league field.

Population size is no guarantee of success in international rugby league. England and France, with populations of around 59 million and 66 million respectively, have already been eliminated. Yet Tonga, home to just 105,000 people, has reached the men’s semi-finals.

The Cook Islands, with fewer than 15,000 residents, is the smallest country represented at the tournament. Although the Cook Islands is not in the semi-finals, seven players across the remaining squads have previously represented this proud nation, including Kiwi stars Charnze Nicoll-Klokstad and Apii Nicholls.
Generations of migration across Te Moana Nui a Kiwa (the Pacific Ocean) and the Tasman Sea have created deep family ties between these countries.

In the women’s semi-finals, 57% of players were born in Australia and another 28% in New Zealand. Twelve players across the Kiwi Ferns and Samoa squads have previously represented other countries, highlighting the overlapping national ties within Pacific rugby league.

The Australia-Fiji semi-final, meanwhile, presents a different picture. Only one Jillaroos player in the final team list, Tiana Penitani Gray, has previously represented another country (Tonga), while none of Fiji’s players have done so.

Club affiliations show a similar concentration in Australia: 86% of players across the four women’s semi-final squads compete in the National Rugby League Women’s Premiership (NRLW). They are based mostly with Australian clubs, though seven play with New Zealand’s Warriors Women. Fiji is the only team to draw heavily on players from outside the competition.

In the men’s semi-finals, 95% of players were born in Australia (50%) or New Zealand (45%). Seventeen players in the NZ-Tonga squads have previously represented another country, while just two players across the four men’s semi-final teams compete outside the National Rugby League (NRL).
The strong presence of NRL and NRLW players also highlights the sporting opportunities available in Australia and New Zealand, and the increasingly diverse populations of both countries.
We see such trends in wider migration patterns. In 2023, Australia and New Zealand recorded net migration gains, while Tonga, Samoa and Fiji experienced net losses.

Another notable demographic trend is the relatively young populations of Pacific nations. As governments around the world prepare for ageing populations and growing demand for services and pensions, the Pacific remains comparatively youthful.
That’s interestingly mirrored in the World Cup squads.

In the women’s competition, New Zealand (median age 27 years) and Australia (26) have considerably older squads than Fiji and Samoa (both 22). The pattern is similar among the men, with New Zealand (29) and Australia (28) fielding older squads than Samoa (26) and Tonga (24).

The differences are even more pronounced in the wider populations. The median ages of New Zealanders (37) and Australians (38) are much higher than those of people in Fiji (28), Tonga (21) and Samoa (20).
Within New Zealand, we can point to a similar pattern. The median age of NZ Europeans is 42, compared with 29 for Fijian New Zealanders, 24 for Samoan New Zealanders and 22 for Tongan New Zealanders.
These younger populations offer what we call a “demographic dividend”: the potential economic benefits as a growing share of the population enters its working and income-earning years.
But these benefits aren’t automatic. Realising them requires investment in young people’s health, education and skills, as well as opportunities to develop their talents and aspirations.
When talent meets opportunity

Many players representing Pacific nations in this weekend’s semi-finals grew up a long way from the islands they now represent. They and their families were drawn to Australia and New Zealand by opportunities in education, employment and sport.

Yet when the chance came, many chose to wear the jersey that reflects their identity, family ties and culture. Their achievements show what’s possible when young people have opportunities to develop their talents.
Building on that momentum means continuing to invest in young people, on and off the field, so the next generation can thrive – wherever they call home.
The authors acknowledge the contribution of Fiu Penjueli, senior statistician, Fiji Bureau of Statistics.

articles.title: What comes after networked authoritarianism?
articles.author: Rebecca MacKinnon
paras: October’s Spotlight contributors illuminated a range of political, economic, and geographic contexts
Originally published on Global Voices
Image by Gerd Altmann on Pixabay.

Fifteen years ago I wrote an article about “networked authoritarianism,” describing China as “exhibit A” for how an authoritarian state adapts to the internet and then adapts digital technologies to increase its own power. I sought to counter prevailing narratives of the time that the internet and tech companies were intrinsically a liberating, democratizing force. While such narratives were eventually discredited, we must not give up on our ability to use technology to defend and exercise our rights. Nor can we simply demand that governments and companies solve the problems they jointly continue to create.

October’s spotlight on Big Tech and Authoritarianism explored a range of relationships between tech companies and political actors across the global majority. Power is wielded through digital technologies in many ways. There are no quick fixes or easy solutions to stop abuses.

But we are not helpless: our Global Voices community has a role to play in strengthening solidarity and cooperation among people fighting to defend their rights, hold abusers accountable, and claim agency over our information environments.

Spotlight contributors illuminated a range of political, economic, and geographic contexts: from Brazil to Hong Kong, Kenya, Myanmar, Palestine, Venezuela, Xinjiang and beyond. They’ve told stories of how different types of governments (or sometimes political insurgents) leverage geopolitical alliances, relationships with tech companies, regulatory power, or other advantages in order to expand political or military dominance, manipulate public opinion, or exercise direct control over citizens. Meanwhile, companies use their own technologies, resources, and government relationships to expand market access and profit.

Tech power is often wielded in ways that make it harder for ordinary people to fight back against abuses. In some cases it is difficult, if not impossible, to prove who has committed what abuse and whether it was intentional — even while harm to individuals or communities has clearly occurred. In other cases, companies discover abuse of their systems to threaten, silence, surveil, or mislead users only after the damage has been done. In Brazil, one expert warns of “governance washing.” An NGO leader working in West Asia and North Africa warns of the rise of a cottage industry of organizations focused on tech accountability without measurably preventing harms.
The dangers of regulation without accountability and public oversight

In North America and Europe, government regulation of Big Tech is often touted as a silver bullet for protecting citizens from harm. But stories from Bangladesh, Kenya and the DRC illustrate different ways that without rigorous safeguards, regulation and enforcement in the name of holding Big Tech accountable can be abused by governments to threaten, track, or discredit critics and political rivals.

Our contributors pointed to conditions that must be met if we are to prevent government abuse of regulations. Laws and regulations need to be evaluated for their compatibility with human rights standards, and reformed or rejected if they fall short. Citizens — through the free press, watchdog NGOs, whistleblower protections and grievance mechanisms — need to be able to monitor and document harms and abuses with clear process for redress and remedy. Sadly, most democracies fail to hold governments — let alone companies — accountable for protecting human rights.

Then there is the even harder problem of what multinational companies should do after a coup or military takeover, leaving users’ data exposed with deadly consequences. Such cases underscore the vital importance of encryption, data security training for civil society, and corporate data minimization practices.
Rejecting techno-imperialism and great power competition

A number of stories describe how global powers leverage their national tech companies to advance strategic and economic interests well beyond their own borders. The companies in turn benefit from such relationships to expand their own global market access, serving as opaque information intermediaries and channels of digital infrastructure.

There has been much media reporting on China’s global tech strategy as a form of its growing soft power. (At the same time, at least one Chinese company insists it is operating independently and should not be treated as an agent of its home government.) But China is not acting alone: It is actually part of a network of authoritarian states, including Russia, Iran, and North Korea, building an international market for digital surveillance. Customers include many countries often described as democracies.

This eye-opening piece points out that, before the U.S. removal of Venezuelan strongman Nicolás Maduro, then vice president and now interim president Delcy Rodrígues negotiated a deal with the Chinese company iFlytek to jointly develop artificial intelligence. That company has been under U.S. sanctions since 2019, but Australian researchers identified layers of Chinese technology deployed across Venezuela. A UN fact finding mission confirmed that they remain in use despite the interim government’s close relationship with the current U.S. presidential administration.

Meanwhile, this article delves into the consequences of global market competition between the U.S. and China. While highly subsidized Chinese ICT infrastructure brings extra benefits to governments that fear their own people, in many cases Chinese tech is the only affordable option. U.S. reciprocal trade agreements that compel countries to restrict purchases of non-U.S. approved infrastructure may make it harder for signatory countries to bridge their own digital divides — which is another way of disempowering their own citizens by keeping digital services out of reach. The piece raises important questions about how countries can assert digital sovereignty to control their own digital infrastructure.
A call for global solidarity

The Chinese government exercises techno-imperialism against its own citizens. Putin’s regime does the same not only at home but in states the Kremlin views as “near abroad.” The articles in October’s spotlight cover events and harms in the global majority. But as I write from San Francisco on the day after U.S. midterm elections, the people of the U.S. are waking up to how the current occupant of the White House and his allies in Silicon Valley have been practicing techno-imperialism on them.

Tech billionaires and trillionaires have been given free rein to maximize profits at the expense of many Americans’ rights and livelihoods, while hyperscaling the government’s ability to surveil, intimidate and imprison. As this chilling piece from Palestine points out, digital surveillance technologies that are first tested in contexts of military occupation, conquest, and even genocide can be — and are — sold and deployed everywhere that governments can get away with doing so.

Several pieces in the series point to open source, decentralized, and community governed technologies as an antidote to Big Tech, exploitation and weaponization. The challenge lies with finding resources and solid legal footing to build out such technologies and systems — especially when so many governments prefer corporate partners as convenient instruments of control and influence. The good news is that cross-border networks of technologists and grassroots organizations are increasingly collaborating around an alternative vision in which communities have agency over their own information environments.

Networked authoritarianism is a global problem. We will only defeat it with global solidarity. As the African-American voting rights activist Fanny Lou Hamer said in 1971: Nobody’s free until everyone’s free.

articles.title: Unmarried Chinese women are rewriting the marriage script
articles.author: Lina Ma
paras: Chinese women are challenging marriage pressures and redefining what it means to be single.
Originally published on Global Voices
The marriage market at People’s Park in Shanghai, 2013. Photo by Jpbowen via Wikimedia Commons, licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0.

On weekends at Shanghai’s People’s Park, umbrellas covered with handwritten sheets of paper line the paths. Parents stand beside them, exchanging information about their unmarried children: age, height, education, income, and whether they own an apartment. It is one of China’s most famous marriage markets — a place where private hopes and social expectations meet in public since 2005.
For years, the word shengnü (剩女), literally translated as “leftover women,” hovered over many of the women whose profiles appeared there.

The translation sounds strange in English because the original Chinese carries a sharper meaning. The character sheng (剩) does not simply mean “remaining.” It suggests something left behind, something unused. In everyday contexts, it can describe leftover food — something that has passed its ideal moment and may eventually be discarded.

When the term became popular in China in the late 2000s, it was used to describe unmarried urban women, often highly educated professionals, who were considered “too old” for marriage after their late twenties. The label was not just a description of marital status. It turned a personal choice into a social judgment.

But today, if you search Chinese media, the phrase shengnü appears far less frequently than it once did. Instead, a more neutral term, zhonggnü (中女), literally translated as “middle or in-and-between women,” is now more often used to describe unmarried women in their thirties in both mainstream media and social platforms.

While the word has faded, many of the expectations behind it remain. The language around unmarried women has become more circumspect, though still pointed. Instead of openly calling women “leftover,” conversations often appear in softer forms: concerns about women being “too picky,” warnings about missing the “best age” for marriage and childbirth, or questions about why a successful woman still has not found a partner.

Instead of using the neutral term zhonggnü, which still highlights women’s age, some women have created new terms and spaces on social media platforms, such as Xiaohongshu and Douban, to discuss these pressures on their own terms. For example, they have reframed the marriage debate to cuīhūn (催婚) — the repeated pressure from family members to marry — and kǒnghūn (恐婚) — the fear or hesitation surrounding marriage itself.
These words reveal a shift. The conversation is no longer only about why women are failing to meet expectations. Increasingly, women are asking whether those expectations should be followed at all.

On Xiaohongshu, a user writing under the name “十元尼美” (Ten Yuan Nimei) described seven years of pressure to marry, beginning when she graduated from university. By 30, she wrote, the pressure had eased — not because her family had accepted her choices, but because people arranging introductions considered her too old for the matchmaking market. At 34, she said, her parents had almost stopped asking.

Her advice to other women began with creating physical distance. Moving from her home province of Hunan to Beijing had largely confined her parents’ pressure to phone calls; later, she moved to Spain. “Sometimes, freedom comes not from persuasion, but from distance,” she wrote.

Other posts question the pressure itself. One shared by the account “渭北春天树” carried the title —“Pressuring someone to marry is, at its core, a form of expulsion.” (催婚的本质是一种驱逐) These conversations no longer see shengnü or unmarried women as a problem, but are turning the conversation on its head to scrutinize traditional conservative family values.

Some women have even embraced and reclaimed the characterization of shengnü as a form of empowerment. Online, some social media posts explicitly recast the label through a play on Chinese characters: 剩, meaning “leftover,” becomes 胜, meaning “victorious,” with the same pronunciation, shèng. A Xiaohongshu post shared by an account named “Kevin” declares: “I’m not a ‘leftover woman’; I’m a ‘victorious woman.’” It advocates remaining single rather than settling, pursuing personal growth, and enjoying time alone.

In another post, the creator “小李存钱记” addresses her mother’s worries about her being unmarried at 30. “I’m not a leftover woman! I’m a victorious woman!” reads the text across the image. She describes juggling several jobs and building an online following, presenting her work and earnings as evidence of her worth. The reframing rejects marriage as the measure of success, while placing considerable emphasis on professional achievement and financial independence.

These posts do not erase the social stigma of the term shengnü. Rather, they show how users are challenging the label by questioning family pressure, sharing ways to escape it, or replacing “leftover” with “victorious.” Yet the language of victory raises another question. If an unmarried woman must point to her earnings, career, or independence to defend her choices, how much room is there simply to be single?

articles.title: Black Michiganders helped push Abdul El-Sayed to victory – but the numbers show he was less popular with this key voting bloc than some other Democratic candidates
articles.author: Christine Slaughter, Assistant Professor of Political Science, Boston University
paras: Progressive Abdul El-Sayed’s victory in Michigan’s U.S. Senate race was one of the most-watched contests in the 2026 midterm elections.

As the results for this race came in, I had my eye on one demographic: Black voters. I am a political scientist who studies Black political behavior. My research has been published in numerous journals, as well as in my forthcoming book, “Black Resilience,” which examines Black voters’ political participation.

The support of Black voters for El-Sayed was not a given. In the August primary, 62% of Detroit voters chose U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens over El-Sayed. Many pundits predicted it would be difficult for El-Sayed to gain support in Detroit, which is about 75% Black.

After the primary, El-Sayed made overtures by sharing his plans to improve the lives of Black Americans, which included supporting the growth of minority-owned businesses, creating more affordable housing, eliminating food deserts and expanding the Rx Kids cash assistance program nationwide.

About 91.8% of Detroit voters supported El-Sayed in the general election, according to the city’s unofficial results. Detroit City Clerk Janice Winfrey said 209,924 residents voted in the 2026 midterms, up about 21% from the 2022 midterm elections. For the 2024 presidential election, 247,770 city residents cast a ballot.
In fact, El-Sayed received 70.6% of Wayne County votes, which includes Detroit. In 2024, Kamala Harris received 62.7% of the vote in Wayne County.
Statewide support is holding steady
In the 2024 presidential election, Michigan’s Democratic vote share fell to 48.3%, from 50.6% in 2020, as the state went for Donald Trump instead of Democratic nominee Harris.

Despite their ideological differences, Sen. Elissa Slotkin and El-Sayed drew similar support among Black voters. In 2024, Slotkin – a moderate Democrat – won 48.6% of the vote, a small margin over Mike Rogers, who was the Republican candidate in that race. In 2026, El-Sayed defeated Rogers statewide by a substantially wider margin, winning 52% of the vote.

In other words, these early election results do not indicate whether Black voters embraced El-Sayed’s progressive platform or simply voted for the Democratic candidate. Voters may have been rejecting Republican Party politics or expressing anger toward Trump over pocketbook issues.

Researchers from Michigan State University found that precincts with more than 80% of Black voters supported Democratic statewide candidates over Republicans at a rate of 92% to 94% during the 2024 general election, which is only slightly lower than the 94% to 95% levels observed in similar precincts during the 2020 contest between Trump and Joe Biden.

Even while Black voters overwhelmingly support Democrats, small shifts in their support and turnout can influence the outcome of close and competitive races. These shifts may help explain differing outcomes, including El-Sayed’s victory in 2026 and Harris’ defeat there in 2024.

While Black voter support for El-Sayed was high, estimated at around 86% statewide, Gov. Gretchen Whitmer’s support among Black voters was about 94% in the 2022 gubernatorial race, according to an ABC exit poll.

Similarly, preelection polling indicated that Jocelyn Benson, the Democratic nominee for governor, polled more favorably among nonwhite voters compared to El-Sayed. NBC exit poll data shows that 86% of Black voters in Michigan supported El-Sayed, while 90% supported Benson, who won the governorship over Republican John James.
Black voters are often strategic voters who support the candidate they believe best aligns with Black interests, which has usually been the Democratic candidate since the Civil Rights Movement.
Generally, Black voters have made their electoral choices based on what’s believed to be best for the group as a whole – a concept described by political scientist Michael C. Dawson as linked fate.

However, recent research shows that Black social networks and institutions, including churches and civic organizations, reinforce expectations of political solidarity. Weaker ties to these networks may lessen the social pressure that encourages Black Americans to participate in politics and support Democratic candidates.

Lower participation by Black Americans could lead to elected officials paying less attention to issues important to Black voters, such as affordability and the cost of living, healthcare, and reducing racial discrimination. If officials assume Black voters will remain loyal to Democrats, they’re under less pressure to win their votes by addressing their concerns.
My research has demonstrated that after the 2024 election, Black women in particular felt frustrated with the Democratic Party, yet they participated in elections despite these frustrations.

El-Sayed was part of a field of notable Democratic candidates in this election cycle. For example, Angie Nixon, a state representative in Florida, championed affordability alongside a moratorium on evictions and a universal jobs program, while James Talarico, a former schoolteacher in Texas, focused on public education.

El-Sayed is a former public health official who had not previously held elected office. This may have turned off some Black voters who often value governing experience. El-Sayed advocated for Medicare For All and lowering the costs of gas prices and groceries.

Although he doesn’t identify as a democratic socialist, El-Sayed campaigned with several progressive elected officials, such as U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders endorsed El-Sayed on the day he announced his candidacy in 2025. El-Sayed also campaigned with the Black establishment, including U.S. Rep. Jim Clyburn of South Carolina. Former President Barack Obama spoke at a rally for El-Sayed in Detroit in October 2026.

Stevens, who lost the Democratic nomination to El-Sayed in the primary, endorsed Republican Mike Rogers after she attended a service with the Republican candidate at a predominantly Black church in Detroit two days before the election. Stevens’ tactic drew severe backlash from Democratic leaders and may have mobilized some Black voters to turn out for El-Sayed on Election Day.
“I felt like she pimped my community,” one Black voter from Detroit told ABC News in response to Stevens’ last-minute endorsement of Rogers.

articles.title: A fractious campaign heralds a cliffhanger election: what to watch as NZ votes
articles.author: Grant Duncan, Research Associate, Public Policy Institute, University of Auckland, Waipapa Taumata Rau
paras: New Zealand First leader Winston Peters – a veteran of 18 general elections – has called this long and sometimes fractious campaign “the worst of my career, easily”. But whether you agree with him or not, tomorrow night still promises exciting live entertainment.

Will Prime Minister Christopher Luxon and his three-party coalition be removed from office after just one term? Will they be replaced by a left-wing coalition led by Labour’s Chris Hipkins – the same man who lost to Luxon in 2023?
Will the Opportunity Party make it over the 5% threshold for seats in parliament, potentially holding the balance of power?
More technically, will the various campaigns to have voters split their two available votes (one for their electorate candidate, one for their preferred party) have a bearing on the result?

Normally in New Zealand’s mixed member proportional (MMP) system, the election numbers that really count are the party-vote percentages. This time, however, individual electorates will matter more than usual.
With polls promising a very tight race, here are some numbers and possible scenarios to track on the night.
Overhangs on the left or right
A parliamentary overhang happens when a party wins more local electorate seats than it would have been awarded in proportion with its percentage of the party vote.
The overhang seats are added (above parliament’s normal 120) to accommodate those extra winners of single-member districts. Overhangs of one to three seats have occurred before.
But this election campaign has seen organised efforts on both the left and right to deliberately use the overhang rule to increase the number of seats their respective sides can win.

Te Pāti Māori is ignoring the party vote entirely and asking supporters to deliver wins in the Māori electorates but give their party vote to Labour or the Greens (which would increase the overall party vote on the left).

Winning three to five Māori electorates would greatly outweigh Te Pāti Māori’s party vote entitlement, which could go below 1%. The number of overhang seats produced on the left will be a major talking point on the night.
A counter-strategy on the right (not officially endorsed by the National Party) assumes National can win more electorates than its party vote (possibly below 30%) would warrant.

The campaign is asking right-wing voters to keep the left-wing parties out of office by party-voting ACT or New Zealand First, and giving electorate votes to the National candidates. By some calculations, if that works, it significantly increases the odds of a right-coalition victory.
Tactical voting and skewed results

It’s impossible to predict how many voters will heed the calls for tactical vote splitting. In the 2023 election, 35.51% of voters split their votes, compared to 27.33% in 2020. National voters were the least likely to do so.
Nonetheless, the overall impact of these opposing strategies to maximise the overhang could increase the size of the next parliament and alter the balance of power.
On the night, watch the numbers of electorate seats won by National and Te Pāti Māori.

In 2023, National won 44 electorates and 38.1% of the party vote. Five MPs from the party list then made up its proportional share of seats. If National’s party vote falls to around 30% this time, we’d normally expect its number of electorate seats to fall, too – maybe below 30.
But if ACT and New Zealand First voters do split their votes, National could win more local electorate seats than the party vote would normally deliver overall.
If National wins 29% of the party vote, for example, that would normally entitle it to 35 seats. Predictions are hazardous, but National could conservatively win 39 or more electorates.

One peculiar outcome could be that Labour gets a higher party vote than National, but National wins more seats than Labour. That’s the kind of disproportionate outcome that brought the old first-past-the-post system into disrepute after the 1978 and 1981 elections.
Opportunity and uncertainty
The next number to watch is the Opportunity Party’s party-vote percentage. Polls indicate it will make it over the 5% threshold for seats in parliament for the first time.

That’s no guarantee – polls are often wrong. But if it does, Opportunity could hold the balance of power after the election. The party’s stated inability to work with New Zealand First (especially after the Michael Laws fiasco) could significantly affect coalition negotiations.

The combined party votes of National and Labour will be another key factor. Since the MMP system began in 1996, that number hasn’t gone below 62%. The lowest was 62.03% in 1996, and the highest was 81.3% in 2017.
Going by opinion polls, that sum may go below 60% this time – the flip side being that smaller parties stand to gain.
In 2023, the Greens won 11.6% of the party vote, ACT 8.6% and NZ First 6.1%. If the polls are more or less correct, all three will get a boost. This, too, could be aided by tactical vote splitting.
Be ready to wait for a result
And we mustn’t forget election-night numbers are only provisional. There are still special votes to count, and there were over 600,000 of those in 2023.
In recent elections, the Greens and Labour have picked up one or two seats between election night and the final count, at the expense of National.
And electorate cliffhangers can be important, too, including maybe one or two Māori seats. Small shifts in seat numbers over the following three weeks could affect prospects for government formation.

The final tally takes three weeks, with coalition negotiations between the parties potentially taking several more. The race isn’t truly won until the governor general swears in a new administration – maybe by Christmas, maybe later.
Although the party that wins the largest percentage of the party vote is normally in pole position to form the next government, that doesn’t necessarily mean they’ll succeed in doing so.
As I write, no one even knows exactly how many seats there will be in parliament – but everything will depend on which workable coalition holds a majority of them.
The leader of the party that comes second may not concede defeat on the night. There may still be everything to play for.

articles.title: What the US midterms result means for the Ukraine war
articles.author: Michael Cox, Founding Director of LSE IDEAS and Emeritus Professor of International Relations, London School of Economics and Political Science
paras: The US midterm elections have shifted the balance of power in Congress, delivering a massive blow to Donald Trump and his Republican party. This has implications both at home and possibly abroad, including for US policy towards Ukraine; an issue that was hardly mentioned during the campaigns.

But even if Ukraine did not figure much in the election, the question in US politics of what to do about the war has not gone away. Indeed, in the weeks and months before the result was announced, Trump had been busily rowing back on US support for Ukraine. This was despite much opposition, even from some Republicans.
Crucial intelligence to Kyiv about Russian strikes was cut off, before later being reinstated, while critical military aid was reduced. Trump also decided to suspend several sanctions on Russia.

This move was denounced by President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine as only helping Russia, but justified by Trump as being “in the national interests of the United States” and also a decision that might help his party’s electoral chances by reducing gas prices.

In the end, none of this helped Trump and the Republicans. Yet few commentators believe that the midterm results, disastrous though they have been for Trump, will have very much impact on his foreign policy outlook and his policy towards Ukraine in particular.

“The Trump administration’s foreign policy is like a car going down the highway,” said James Green, a research fellow at the Centre for European Reform and former Congressional aide in Washington, recently. “Congress has the ability to slow that car down, maybe make it put on a turn signal, but it’s going to be very difficult for Congress to change the overall route over the next two years.”

In part, this has to do with how foreign policy is determined in the US. Congress is not without some influence. It can hold hearings, subpoena executive branch officials, as well as exercise control over the purse. Yet as commander-in-chief and head of state with a vast foreign policy bureaucracy supporting him, the president retains significant foreign policy powers.

The Democrats are also unlikely to make Ukraine front and centre after the midterms. They will have other more important fish to fry, the most critical being how to make sure they come up with a candidate and programme that will win them the White House in 2028.

Yet Ukraine is a cause which many Democrats and quite a few Republicans have championed for some time. Nor are they likely to forget what ordinary Americans think about Russia and its leader, Vladimir Putin.

The war in Ukraine may not be something they think about on a daily basis. On the other hand, as the Pew Research Center showed in 2025, 67% of Americans distrust Putin while six in ten view Russia as an enemy.

Democrats may not wish to become embroiled in a European war. But having just scored a sweeping landslide victory, they may well calculate there is a good deal of political mileage to be had now in escalating their attack on a weakened Trump if his foreign policy towards Russia and Ukraine continues in their view to reward an aggressor while making the victim of that aggression look like an obstacle to a settlement.

If the midterms result presents a series of opportunities for the Democrats, while posing a challenge to Trump, it also presents Putin with a possible opportunity. The Russian leader may well try and exploit Trump’s domestic position by offering some kind of settlement that would allow the US president to claim a victory.

US, Chinese and Russian officials have already been holding talks about a summit when the heads of state travel to China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit later in November. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov has said Russia hopes to finalise the meeting in the coming days.

Trump is similarly keen on such a meeting. He told reporters in October that Ukraine would be discussed at the meeting, adding: “I would meet in order – anything I can do to end the war, whether somebody is there or not, whatever I can do to end the war.”

This might sound reasonable enough. However, deciding the fate of a sovereign country which won’t be at the negotiating table, and coming to some kind of “great power” deal with two authoritarian countries that involves Ukraine losing 20% of its territory, is almost certainly something an emboldened Democratic party in Congress will not take lying down.

Nor, according to most military experts, would it be wise to concede anything to Russia when its war against Ukraine appears to have run into the ground. According to the Institute for the Study of War, Russia may have “secured a temporary advantage in the skies over Ukraine through their jet-powered drones and the shortage of Patriot missiles that can intercept their ballistic missiles”.

But as the institute also points out, unless western military aid dries up entirely, a Russian victory is by no means inevitable. A war that most experts, including the CIA, predicted would be over in a matter of months is thus likely to go on.

Trump is unlikely to change his mind about Russia and Ukraine. Russia in his mind’s eye will continue to be regarded as a potential partner, and Ukraine a country that has taken assistance from the US and given “absolutely nothing back except grief”.

But now, with his back to the wall politically and the Democrats in charge of Congress in a country that has just passed a decisive verdict on his presidency, shaping his own agenda in relation to Russia and Ukraine is likely to prove more difficult.
Michael Cox was a founding director of LSE IDEAS and is an associate fellow at Chatham House.

articles.title: Why Québec separatism is unlikely despite the Parti Québecois election win
articles.author: Gavin Furrey, Assistant Professor, Political Science, Université du Québec à Montréal (UQAM)
paras: Québec’s flagship sovereignist party, the Parti Québecois (PQ), formed a minority government in the recent provincial election. The party essentially rose from the dead after a 12-year absence, dethroning the right-wing nationalist — but not separatist — Coalition Avenir Québec (CAQ).

For Canadians, the PQ is typically associated with sovereignty referendums. Yet, despite the PQ victory, estimates place Québecois support for sovereignty at between 27 and 31 per cent, a far cry from the 49.42 per cent who voted to separate in the 1995 referendum.
This figure aligns somewhat with the popular vote received by the PQ, which, at 28 per cent, is the lowest popular vote share of a sitting government in the history of the province.

The PQ’s victory therefore should be understood in light of three factors: low public support for the PQ and for separatism, Indigenous resistance to Québec independence and a global context where statehood doesn’t necessarily shield against interference or expand diplomatic leverage.
Lukewarm mood on independence
The combination of Québec’s multi-party system and its “first-past-the-post” electoral system means governments are often formed on less than a majority of the popular vote.
In six elections between 2007–2022, an average of 53.9 per cent of votes failed to translate into seats, according to electoral expert Mercédez Roberge.
This explains how the separatist PQ was able to form government despite the measured lack of enthusiasm for separatism in the province.

In fact, even leaving room for the possibility that leftist Québec Solidaire supporters also support independence (though the party does not necessarily prioritize it), a combination of the popular votes earned by parties that explicitly do not support independence suggests that 58.24 per cent of the electorate don’t want to separate from Canada.

PQ leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon’s statements following his party’s victory reflects a generally lukewarm mood towards independence in the province. During his campaign, Plamondon mitigated his promise to hold a referendum during his first term by stating it wouldn’t be held while Donald Trump remained president of the United States.
In the meantime, Plamondon has prioritized housing and cost of living issues, and has signalled to the English-speaking community that “we’re all in the same boat.”
Plamondon’s prudence is paired with various assertions of Québec autonomy.

In his first month as premier, he’s antagonized the federal government by skipping the recent Canada-European Union summit. Under the CAQ, antagonism was more often directed at Québec’s increasingly ethnically and religiously diverse population. Without dropping this inward-facing orientation to nation-building, the PQ’s swipes at Ottawa suggests it will return to stoking more familiar Québec-Ottawa tensions.

But in a country with longstanding debates about provincial autonomy, none of this is new or indicative of separatist sentiments. The recent PQ victory is more akin to detecting a faint pulse in a terminally ill patient than a spectacular jolt back to life.
The PQ has formed a government in a situation different from 1995.

Domestically, First Nations have increasingly affirmed their place in Canada’s tapestry. In 1996, the Royal Commission on Aboriginal Peoples published its five-volume, 4,000-page report making 440 recommendations. Among them were recognizing Indigenous Peoples as self-governing nations and creating Indigenous institutions, including an Indigenous parliament.

In 2015, the Truth and Reconciliation Commission published its final report, which included 94 calls to action to address the harms of the residential school system and advance reconciliation across areas that include child welfare, education, health, justice and culture.

The following year, Canada officially adopted the United Nations Declaration for the Rights of Indigenous Peoples. The document became federal law in 2021. Finally, since 1995, at least 19 modern treaties have been concluded or come into effect.
It would be misleading to claim, however, that the relationship between Canadian governments and Indigenous nations has radically changed in the last 30 years.

Plamondon’s absence from the First Nations-First Ministers meeting recently held in Ottawa is an example. Québec’s minister responsible for relations with First Nations and Inuit wrote that the premier’s absence was aimed at prioritizing direct nation-to-nation meetings with Indigenous nations on “notre territoire (‘our territory.’)”

This phrasing takes Québec’s territorial sovereignty as a given, treating it as a non-negotiable precondition that other nations must accept before dialogue can even begin. By prioritizing provincial self-determination, it implicitly subordinates Indigenous sovereignty.
Claiming these talks are “nation-to-nation” rings hollow when one party unilaterally dictates the terms of engagement.

The premier’s decision to skip the meeting was criticized by the Assembly of First Nations of Québec and Labrador (AFNQL) and the Native Women’s Shelter of Montréal, who wanted Québec to be at the table in Ottawa.

Plamondon would do well to remember that in 1995, multiple First Nations within Québec’s boundaries refused forcible inclusion into a new independent state, notably those whose rivers provide the bulk of the province’s hydroelectricity.
Modern risks of independent statehood

Internationally, separatist sentiments today have more to do with populism than with the decolonization efforts that played out in the second half of the 20th century. In a climate of survival-of-the-fittest foreign policy, sovereignty in the form of an independent state does not guarantee the same freedoms or capacities it might have in 1980 and 1995.

As U.K. political scientist Michael Keating suggests, self-determination is no longer fixed to a single people or territory. Nations today are largely regarded as contested constructs, and territories are multi-layered with various cultural and ethnic populations.
Additionally, sovereignty doesn’t shield a state from the decisions of another, as recent American tariff policies are showing Canadians all too well.

Keating’s argument aligns with Indigenous political theories of relational autonomy: today sovereignty is experienced less as something a nation possesses and more as a continuously negotiated relationship.

American threats to Canadian sovereignty and Greenland’s self-determination suggests that secession would not necessarily improve upon Québec’s ability to negotiate its position within the broader international order.

In short, in a world where even the U.S., a superpower for decades, is experiencing the costs of fractured relationships, a convincing pitch for Québec separatism would have to take into account similar costs. The pulse of Québec separatism persists, though the body sustaining it is weighed down by internal fractures and a punishing political landscape.

articles.title: Delayed international support has hampered efforts to contain and treat Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo
articles.author: Olayinka Stephen Ilesanmi, Assistant Professor of Healthcare Administration, Fayetteville State University
paras: I visited a family of 19 in Sierra Leone in 2015. By the time I arrived, eight had died. The other 11 were left to live with the grief and fear of what might happen next.

I am a medical doctor and epidemiologist, and at that time I was serving on an African Union Ebola response mission. The 2014-16 epidemic in West Africa caused more than 28,600 cases and 11,300 deaths. Over roughly six months in Sierra Leone, I saw how quickly the disease could overwhelm families and health services.

That’s also when I learned that good medical advice can fail if people do not trust those delivering it. Some families buried relatives secretly, despite warnings. In certain communities, funeral practices included washing the body and sprinkling water on mourners, which risked exposing people to infected bodily fluids.

Simply repeating instructions did not help. But those of us working in the field found that working with families to make burials safer while respecting their grief helped them to mourn their loss while stopping the virus from spreading.

More than a decade later, those experiences have returned to my mind. The Ebola outbreak now sweeping across parts of Central Africa is different from the one I responded to. Still, one lesson remains: Timely international support makes a huge difference.

The current outbreak was declared in the Democratic Republic of Congo, or DRC, in May 2026. By Oct. 28, 2026, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported 10,305 confirmed cases and 4,996 deaths across five countries, with new updates daily. The DRC accounts for nearly all of those cases and deaths.
This is already the second-largest Ebola outbreak ever recorded, after the 2014-16 epidemic.
The current outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, whereas the 2014-16 epidemic involved a different Ebola virus. No vaccine or specific treatment is currently approved for Bundibugyo.
The World Health Organization warns that late detection, deaths outside health facilities and sustained transmission in the DRC remain serious concerns.

The DRC has extensive experience with responding to outbreaks, and African institutions are coordinating a continental response. Africa has the expertise and leadership. What it needs right now is sustained support that reaches the front line – quickly, safely and accountably.
Ebola follows human movement. In October, Kenya reported infections linked to a traveler who had passed through Uganda from the DRC. Nigeria also reported an imported case around the same time.
Symptoms can appear between two and 21 days after exposure, and people are generally not infectious before symptoms begin. A traveler may therefore pass a temperature check and become ill days later.
These events show why countries need to share information quickly, verify travel histories and maintain contact tracing across borders.
What international support looks like now

International partners are, in fact, contributing. In September 2026, the United States reported US$887 million in Ebola-related health and humanitarian assistance. The U.K. announced a contribution of roughly £78 million ($104 million).

In October, the World Bank described $426.6 million in current and planned financing for the DRC and neighboring countries. And Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention reported nearly $3 billion in international pledges following a September mobilization effort.
But pledges are not the same as supplies delivered or services provided, and these contributions are coming late in the outbreak.

In 2014, Britain helped expand treatment and safe-burial operations in Sierra Leone. The U.S. mobilized logistics capacity in Liberia, while France assisted Guinea. And African Union health workers served alongside local teams and other partners.

That cooperation saved lives, though the global response was slow to scale up. It has been discouraging for me to see that today’s response has not built on that experience without waiting for the outbreak to grow further.
According to the WHO, massive cuts to international aid over the past year diminished a quicker response.

The success of international collaboration will be measured in how many contacts are reached, how rapidly patients are tested, how many health workers have protective equipment and are consistently paid, whether women can still deliver babies safely, and whether remote communities can get care.
Building connections with everyday people

My experience in Sierra Leone in 2014 taught me that trust is essential to outbreak control. Families need credible explanations, timely information and opportunities to ask questions. Local health workers, faith leaders, survivors and community organizations can help bridge the gap between an emergency response and the people it seeks to protect.

That gap can be large even when a disease is widely known. A colleague and I conducted a study involving 440 secondary school students in Nigeria in 2014, and we found that 95.4% had heard of Ebola. Yet only 42.3% identified fever as a possible symptom, and only 33.2% recognized the risk associated with certain burial practices. Seeing that awareness of the disease alone was not enough, we subsequently began Ebola education activities in local Nigerian schools.

The need for reliable information from trusted sources remains in 2026. Risk messages must be consistent, culturally sensitive and practical. This works only when communities are partners in recognizing illness, seeking early care, contact follow-up and safe, dignified burials. Even in times of emergency, health workers cannot treat communities simply as audiences for instructions.
Reaching affected communities
In August 2026, Africa CDC and the WHO jointly called for expanded laboratory and treatment capacity and faster delivery of supplies.

But in the DRC, insecurity and displacement due to ongoing conflict, in addition to poor roads, can prevent supplies and patients from reaching treatment centers. These obstacles may also keep laboratories from receiving samples and contact-tracing teams from visiting households.

The ministry of health is not equipped to resolve these problems. The response therefore requires cooperation among health authorities, humanitarian agencies, local government, transport services and those responsible for civilian safety.

There are signs that investments in these services are helping. In October, the World Bank reported that supported detection timelines in the DRC had improved. This meant new cases were being detected within one or two days by September, a huge improvement from the 10-day detection timeline early in the outbreak.

Because Bundibugyo virus lacks an approved vaccine or specific treatment, this outbreak also demands carefully conducted research. The Tumaini vaccine trial, begun in Bunia, DRC, in October 2026, is an important step toward a potential vaccine.
The hope is that this effort will prevent more families from experiencing loss.
I still remember the 11 survivors in that Sierra Leone household I visited back in 2015. I never learned what ultimately happened to them, but more than a decade later, I still think about them.
Olayinka Stephen Ilesanmi was the past West Africa Regional Program Lead for Africa CDC.

articles.title: Young men and Latino voters helped drive the Democrats’ blue wave. Why did they abandon Trump?
articles.author: Grace Jennings-Edquist, Executive Producer, Podcasts, The Conversation
paras: The young men and Hispanic and Latino voters who helped propel Donald Trump to his presidential victory in 2024 swung sharply towards the Democrats in the midterm elections, contributing to the historic defeat for Republicans.

Charles Hunt, an associate professor of political science at Boise State University in Idaho, tells The Conversation Weekly podcast that the results suggest weakened support for Trump and his MAGA movement among these key groups of voters.

Hispanic and Latino voters “swung heavily towards Trump in 2024”, Hunt says. But midterm results in Florida, Texas and elsewhere “are showing these voters just slingshotting completely in the other direction,” he explains, citing early exit polls and analysis by The New York Times.

Not just back towards where they were in, say, 2018 or 2020 in terms of support for Democrats, but past that – being more supportive of folks like James Talarico in Texas than they have been of any Democrat in the last 20 years. That’s really, really significant, especially since that’s a growing part of the electorate.

The New York Times’ analysis of voting trends reveals young voters swung back toward the Democratic Party by more than 30 percentage points – the largest shift of any age group. Young men, in particular, swung strongly back towards the Democrats.
The AP Voter Poll, a sweeping survey of voters across all 50 states, shows Democrats regaining ground among young and Hispanic voters, too.

The scale of the Republicans’ defeat goes beyond the usual midterm backlash against a sitting president, Hunt says. He draws a comparison with the 1974 midterm elections following the Watergate scandal and then-President Richard Nixon’s resignation:
This is a level of […] midterm blowback against an incumbent president of the sort that we haven’t seen since 1974. […] It’s really pretty historic and in a completely different league than 2018.
So what drove voters towards the Democrats?
Economic pressures are one reason, Hunt says. He points to the effects of the Iran war and tariffs, particularly on highly visible costs such as petrol:
A lot of political science tells us that economic issues are almost always front of mind for voters.
But those pressures also gave force to Democratic messaging about corruption and an economy favouring billionaires. He adds:

I think those issues tie together with a lot of Democratic messaging around things like corruption, and the influence of billionaires, and Elon Musk spending half a billion dollars in this election probably did not help, at the end of the day.

articles.title: The Binance hack exploited familiar weaknesses – all organisations should learn from it
articles.author: Bogdan Księżopolski, Head of the Institute of Computer Science, Head of Cybersecurity Department, Kozminski University
paras: Hackers have stolen around US$6.3 billion (£4.7 billion) from the cryptocurrency exchange Binance, most of which was taken in under an hour. According to Binance, the attack exploited systems and individuals with the authority to carry out transactions involving such large sums.

Such vulnerabilities exist everywhere; statistics show that people and the systems they directly use, including their personal computers, remain a top target for cybercriminals. All organisations could therefore learn lessons from this attack.

The Binance theft took place on the evening of October 29, 2026. The Binance attack netted four times the amount stolen in the previous biggest cryptocurrency theft, on the Bybit exchange in February 2025.

Private keys, used to authorise spending or withdrawal from crypto-wallets, are a known vulnerability. But Binance found no evidence these were leaked. An initial statement from the exchange pointed to a compromised laptop belonging to an engineer. This gave the attacker access to the internal system that processes withdrawal requests.

Because blockchain transactions can be fully audited, investigators can trace the events leading up to the attack. On October 28, the address from which the theft was later carried out received 0.3 ETH (Ether cryptocurrency) from Tornado Cash, a service that mixes funds from multiple users to hide their origin.

A few hours before the theft, a malicious smart contract (computer code that automatically runs when certain conditions are met) was deployed from the same address. At 20:20:59 UTC, a transaction was sent from that address containing 50 signed authorisations intended to transfer control of a Binance wallet to that smart contract. One of them was accepted by a Binance hot wallet (a wallet used by the exchange to process customer withdrawals).

Following this takeover, the hackers proceeded to empty the hot wallet of 64 different tokens worth approximately $2.5 billion (£1.8 billion) in a single transaction. Other wallets were then emptied in parallel using standard signed transactions, bringing the total amount stolen to $6.3 billion. Valid Binance digital signatures were needed for draining the wallets, but how the attackers obtained these has not been explained.
The same audit trail shows that the attackers were rehearsing several hours earlier, but at that stage, nothing linked them to Binance.

The 2025 attack on Bybit, which resulted in the theft of US$1.5 billion (£1.1 billion), also appears to have involved a compromised laptop that was capable of performing operations requiring high-level privileges.

North Korean cybercriminals, who were implicated in the attack on the Bybit exchange by analysts, specialise in creating so-called “legends”. These are identities created to deceive companies and individuals. In October, the US Department of Justice indicted 14 individuals in a case in which North Korean cybercriminals, using stolen or fabricated identities, secured remote jobs at more than 70 US companies.

Two days before the attack, Binance reported that, for a week, it had been blocking North Korea-linked attack attempts involving fake recruiters. Was this related to the attack? We don’t know yet, but the modus operandi is well recognised and widespread. North Korea, meanwhile, has denied allegations that it was behind the attack.

A cybercriminal can use a legend to pose for months as a hardworking employee, a cheap and reliable contractor, or as a generous employer. The criminal waits for the moment when a crucial software installation is carried out or a vital document is signed. Since a large amount of today’s work involves only digital interactions with people, it is sensible to approach every new contact with limited trust.

A good example of how such legends work is the attack on the Japanese DMM Bitcoin exchange in 2024, which netted US$308 million (£230 million) for the attackers. The hacker posed as a recruiter on LinkedIn and gained the trust of a Ginco employee.

Ginco is a company that provides DMM with wallet management software. The recruiter offered the Ginco employee a job on the condition that they completed a recruitment test. The test URL actually led to a malicious Python script; from this point on, the victim’s computer was compromised.
This is classic social engineering. In this case, the target was a cryptocurrency wallet system accessed through a compromised computer. About two months later, the attackers drained funds from DMM.

Virtually all businesses should learn from such attacks. The first lesson concerns what their computer systems are allowed to authorise. Traditionally, cryptographic keys are protected using devices known as hardware security modules and multi-signature schemes (where multiple private keys are required to authorise an action).

Unfortunately, such mechanisms do not protect against an attack launched from a compromised internal system controlled by a hacker. It is advisable to define rules for authorising financial transactions, set time and amount limits, and require approval via an alternative channel for unusual requests.

Additionally, since most of the funds in the Binance cyberattack were transferred within an hour, computer systems should have mechanisms in place to block suspicious transactions within seconds, without waiting for approval from the on-duty security engineer.

The second lesson is about recruitment, which has evolved into a security mechanism. North Korean cybercriminals use stolen or fabricated identities and virtual private networks (VPNs) to pose as people living in the US.

Visual identities during online interviews can be falsified using deepfakes. Video interviews and CVs no longer prove who someone really is. In some cases, actors are even hired for in-person interviews. Today, we need to focus on strengthening the identity verification process. It’s important to check candidates through independently verified contacts during this process.

The third lesson concerns the work computers of individuals with privileged access to the computer system. Typically, organisations have protected themselves against phishing through training and email filters.
Unfortunately, some of the attacks described above bypass the filters that are currently in use because they target specific victims (an act known as spear phishing).

In the case of Bybit, gaining access to a developer’s computer allowed the attacker to seize session tokens in the cloud and bypass multi-factor authentication. One possible solution is to separate privileged access from day-to-day operations.

To this end, access to withdrawal systems should only be permitted from company-managed dedicated devices, and computer code received from external sources should only be executed in an isolated environment.

The largest cryptocurrency theft in history is essentially a story about how people and processes are the weakest links in security systems. Cryptography was not compromised and remains a key security measure. Unfortunately, these same vulnerabilities exist in banks, payment companies and hospitals and attackers are well aware of them.
