articles.title: With control of Congress, here’s how Democrats could stop Trump’s war in Iran
articles.author: Markus Wagner, Professor of Law and Director of the UOW Transnational Law and Policy Centre, University of Wollongong
paras: The Democrats’ sweeping victory in the US midterm elections puts them in a stronger position to interfere with President Donald Trump’s agenda. This includes his deeply unpopular and costly war against Iran, which could be among their first priorities.
As president, Trump will be able to veto any legislation aimed at ending the war. But the Democrats still have another powerful card up their sleeves: cutting off funding for the war.

There are caveats, however. History suggests exercising this power could trigger a political confrontation that may backfire. And even if the Democrats succeed in ending the war, they may not be able to reverse the damage it has done to the US’ global standing.
Democrats will have three main options to try to force the war against Iran to a close. Two of these, however, face significant limitations.
The first – and perhaps most obvious – option is through legislation. There are a few different ways to do this.
One approach is to pass a resolution calling for an end to the war.

Congress already attempted this in June, passing a concurrent resolution (with the support of some Republicans) that directed the president to either withdraw US forces from hostilities against Iran or seek the approval of Congress before continuing. This was done under the War Powers Resolution of 1973.

These so-called concurrent resolutions are, however, widely seen as non-binding. Intended to express the opinion or will of Congress, they are generally used to deal with internal matters within Congress.
Trump ignored it. A similar resolution then failed in the Senate in September.

For such a resolution to be binding, it would need the force of a law passed by Congress, which the president would likely veto. To overcome that veto, the Democrats would need the support of a two-thirds majority in both the House and the Senate. This would require a significant number of Republicans to cross the aisle.

A second option for the Democrats is to launch a series of congressional investigations into the way the war has been conducted. This would likely include public hearings, subpoenas and demands for documents from the Trump administration.
The Democrats may also attempt to impeach senior officials in the Trump administration.

If Hakeem Jeffries, the Democrat tipped to become the next speaker of the House, wants to appease some of the more progressive voices in his party – or the hardline voices on the Iran war or against Trump – Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth could be targeted for impeachment.

But the grounds for such proceedings are unclear at this stage, and even with the Democrats’ new Senate majority, he would be unlikely to be convicted unless a significant number of Republicans crossed the aisle.
More pertinently, congressional investigations are a protracted process, and unlikely to bring the war to a swift end.
The more immediate power that Congress has to end the war swiftly is in Article I, Section 9 of the US Constitution, which states:
No Money shall be drawn from the Treasury, but in Consequence of Appropriations made by Law […]
This is known as the “power of the purse”.
Once the new Congress is sworn in in January, every new dollar that Trump’s Department of War wants to spend needs to be approved by the House and the Senate.

A Democrat-controlled Congress could put a clause into the defence budget, prohibiting funds from being used for hostilities against Iran. Trump could veto this, but this would mean blocking the paycheck for everyone in the military, as well.

The Democrats tried this very approach in 2007, attempting to force a timetable for a US withdrawal from Iraq. Then-President George W. Bush vetoed it, but it became a political football, with both sides accusing the other of leaving US troops unfunded.
The Democrats ultimately backed down due to the growing risk of backlash from voters.

Today, this approach would carry a similar risk. Are the Democrats willing to put their political credibility on the line if the president accuses them of letting American soldiers down? Who blinks first?
Republicans face a reckoning

As the dust settled on Wednesday, Trump himself acknowledged the Iran war had played a role in the Republican Party’s crushing defeat. But he doubled down on the decision, saying he would do it all over again if necessary to prevent Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon.

Vice President JD Vance was less defensive. In a detailed statement posted to X, Vance bluntly declared the war was the reason the Republicans lost. He added, “any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there”.
Vance has long criticised US military involvement in overseas conflicts, but in his role as vice president has publicly backed Trump’s actions against Iran.
This week’s overwhelming Democratic victory has made it much easier for Vance – and other Republicans – to now break ranks with the president.
The balance of power has shifted
For Trump, bringing the war to an end now would mean humiliation. The US has so far poured almost US$50 billion into a military campaign with few tangible achievements.

On top of that, Iran has learned that the Strait of Hormuz is a chokepoint it can control. The same is true for the Bab al-Mandeb Strait off the coast of Yemen, where the Iran-aligned Houthis have attacked commercial ships.

These costs will outlast the Trump presidency. The war might definitively bring to an end the unipolar global order Washington built after the end of the Cold War. The biggest winner may not be Tehran, but Beijing.
Markus Wagner received funding from the Australian Department of Defence as principal investigator for the Weaponised Trade project.

articles.title: The scandals and suspects surrounding Flávio Bolsonaro, according to the Brazilian press
articles.author: Global Voices Brazil
paras: After being defeated in the elections, the senator fled to the US with his family
Originally published on Global Voices
Art by Global Voices with Canva Pro. Photo by the Brazilian Senate. Fair use.

Forty-eight hours after losing the runoff in Brazil to incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, Flávio Bolsonaro, former president Jair Bolsonaro’s eldest son, a senator representing Rio de Janeiro, fled to the United States. From there, where his brother Eduardo, a former congressman, has lived since February 2025, he continues to challenge the results of the election he lost by 4.4 million votes, as attested by the Electoral Court (TSE), the Organization of American States (OAS), and other right-led governments in the region.

Upon landing in Miami, Flávio published a letter proclaiming himself “the true president of Brazil” and “president-elect of Brazil.” After 22 minutes — and a demand from the US Department of State — he retracted to “the leader of Brazil.”

US President Donald Trump had said that Brazil’s elections “looked rigged,” but he wouldn't “get involved.” The New York Times reported, however, that Flávio was helped by Trump's aides. “The jet [he traveled on] had been arranged by a White House official,” affirmed the newspaper.

Flávio’s narrative is that he is being persecuted by the Brazilian justice system and Lula’s government as an opposition leader, since the Supreme Court ordered the seizure of his passports — he also has Italian citizenship — right after his defeat was announced.

Justice Alexandre de Moraes, considered a foe of the Bolsonaro family and himself under suspicion for having links to the same disgraced banker connected to Flávio, issued the order in response to a Federal Police request that considered Flávio a flight risk. In Brazil, a president cannot be investigated for alleged crimes committed before their term, meaning that once elected, all pending investigations involving Flávio would have been suspended. This is also the first time in 24 years that Flávio will not have a seat to ensure his parliamentary immunity.

According to the Brazilian Federal Police, three elements indicated a flight risk in Flávio’s case: an interview his brother Eduardo gave to a podcast in the US defending the idea of him leaving the country, on October 23, his considerable economic power, and well-established structures abroad that could support him in a long stay.

The day after the election, after visiting his father, who is under house arrest convicted for a coup attempt, Flávio recorded a video complaining about the measure, claiming “he never thought about leaving the country” and promising to stay and answer to investigations. Overnight, apparently, he had a change of heart in time for a new plan.

Investigations and corruption suspicions have long surrounded his name. In 2020, Sergio Moro, the judge who convicted Lula, resigned as Bolsonaro’s justice minister, accusing the president of trying to intervene with the Federal Police to protect Flávio in an embezzlement and money-laundering inquiry. In a cabinet meeting, then-president Bolsonaro shouted at his ministers: “I won’t wait until they fuck my entire family,” saying he would fire whoever got in their way.

During this election campaign, skeletons in Flávio's closet were further exposed in stories published by the Brazilian press. Global Voices gathered the main ones here. Flávio is currently under three investigations at the Supreme Court.

This is the case that led Jair Bolsonaro to allegedly interfere in the Federal Police in 2020. Flávio was indicted by Rio’s Public Prosecution Office for embezzlement, money laundering, and criminal organization. The case was later adjourned. Rachadinha (“split” in English) is a salary kickback scheme in which a politician hires someone for a certain position and then reclaims part of their salary.

In 2018, after Bolsonaro’s election, a report by the Council for Financial Activities Control (Coaf) pointed to atypical financial movements in the account of Flávio’s aide, Fabricio Queiroz, an old friend of his father. Queiroz, who was filmed paying for Flávio's daughters’ tuition in cash, was identified as the scheme’s operator. For the Public Prosecution Office, according to UOL news outlet, the scheme was used to cover Flávio’s personal expenses and to increase his patrimony.

There were also suspicions that a chocolate franchise shop, owned by Flávio, was used for money laundering. The investigation found 1,512 cash deposits in repeated amounts between March 2015 and December 2018 at the establishment.

An audio recording found by police in 2024 shows then-president Jair Bolsonaro, Flávio’s attorneys, and Alexandre Ramagem, former director of the Brazilian Intelligence Agency (Abin), currently a fugitive living in the US, allegedly discussing a plan to free Flávio from the investigations through Federal Revenue Service employees.

On May 13, 2026, The Intercept Brasil published a story and an audio recording showing that the movie “Dark Horse,” a biopic about Jair Bolsonaro, starring Jim Caviezel, could have been financed by disgraced banker Daniel Vorcaro. Before the story went out, a reporter from the news outlet asked Flávio about the case. The senator laughed and dismissed the question, saying: “That’s a lie! Where did you get this from?”

Vorcaro is at the center of one of the country's biggest scandals, involving politicians, members of the Supreme Court and other judges, and celebrities, through his bank, Master — its license was approved during Jair Bolsonaro’s government. Vorcaro is investigated for a fraud scheme that caused a BRL 47 billion (around USD 8.7 billion) loss to the Credit Guarantee Fund (FGC), which backs Brazil's banking system.

The messages published by The Intercept show Flávio negotiating with Vorcaro on WhatsApp. Flávio asked for BRL 134 million (USD 24.9 million) and received at least BRL 61 million (USD 11.17 million). In one of the last messages between them, before Vorcaro was arrested while trying to flee the country, Flávio tells him: “Brother, I am and will always be with you; there is no half-talk between us,” reported TIB.
Since he couldn’t deny their link, Flávio has repeated that the money he negotiated with Vorcaro was “private money for a private movie.”

This is also one of the investigations into Flávio at the Federal Supreme Court (STF), which targets the movie’s financing operation. Despite the movie being filmed in Brazil, Vorcaro sent the money to a fund in the US (Havengate), managed by a friend of Eduardo Bolsonaro’s. The final destination for the money hasn't been confirmed yet.

Another inquiry investigates Flávio for money laundering and currency evasion, along with his friend Willer Tomaz, a Brazilian lawyer also currently in the US. Tomaz is under investigation for money laundering through betting companies and involvement in another scandal, a fraud scheme at the national pension fund (INSS).
Documents accessed by Brazilian news outlets showed that Tomaz alone moved BRL 5 billion (around USD 930 million) in betting sites and cashed out BRL 200 million (USD 37.2 million).

When Piauí magazine revealed that Flávio had travelled in Vorcaro’s plane with his family, the senator’s first reaction was to say that “fortunately, it was Willer's.” His friend shared the plane’s quotas with a Vorcaro company. Tomaz denied ever meeting with the banker.

In October, O Globo newspaper published that Flávio had been registered as a “master user” on an offshore account under the name of a company managed by Tomaz and registered on Madeira Island, Portugal. This status could give him “significant operational access,” according to the Federal Police. Piauí magazine also says the senator could have been an indirect partner in a betting company based in São Paulo, but controlled by another company registered in Madeira, also linked to Tomaz. Flávio denies it.

Folha de S. Paulo newspaper says that the relationship between Flávio and Tomaz began in 2019. During the COVID-19 parliamentary inquiry commission at the National Congress, two years later, the senator defended Tomaz, calling him a friend. They always denied being business associates, claiming they were only friends.
Ana Clara’s death and the militias

On the morning of February 2, 2021, five-year-old Ana Clara Machado was shot and killed while playing at the doorstep of her home, in Rio de Janeiro. The Military Police denied any confrontation or the presence of narcos in the area where their operation was taking place. Later, the Civil Police identified police officer Bruno Delaroli as the shooter and arrested him. In March, 2026, ICL Notícias, a news website, reported that Flávio Bolsonaro worked on the officer's defense team in the higher courts, trying to avoid a jury trial. Another news outlet, UOL, revealed he worked pro bono. Lula questioned the senator about his motives during a debate on TV Globo.
Also, according to ICL, this wasn’t the only case Flávio advocated for officers accused of killings. Folha says his career as a defense lawyer gained traction after he was elected senator.

During his political life, Flávio has had a long history of links to police officers identified as members of so-called militias — paramilitary groups mostly formed by active and retired officers, carrying out vigilante and organized crime activities in dominated territories. When a state deputy in Rio, Flávio employed at his office the mother and wife of Adriano da Nobrega, an ex-military policeman, linked to a militia known as Crime Office, whose main activities were to execute ordered killings. He also sent parliamentary money to an NGO connected to another police officer involved in the murder of Rio’s city councillor Marielle Franco. According to Piauí magazine, the militia man known as “Peixe” (fish) referred to Flávio as “our senator.”
ICL News says the UN will examine Flávio's links to the militias when analyzing Ana Clara’s case.

articles.title: Tracing the recruitment trap behind Russia’s war
articles.author: Zulker Naeen
paras: No justice for Bangladeshi workers who are recruited into Russia’s war
Originally published on Global Voices
War-wounded Bangladeshis in Russia plead to return home. Screenshot from a YouTube report by Ekhon TV. Fair use.

Maksudur Rahman was 31 when a labor recruiter arrived in his hometown in Lakshmipur district, southeastern Bangladesh, with a job offer: becoming a janitor in Russia. Nearly every family in the district has someone working overseas, so the pitch landed. According to an international investigation, he borrowed money and paid the broker BDT 1.2 million (about USD 9,800). For a household like his, that is a fortune, but the promised wages made the debt look manageable. He signed up and flew out.

What followed had nothing to do with brooms. Within weeks, he was on the front lines of Russia’s war in Ukraine. He and three other Bangladeshi workers were handed a paper written in Russian — a language they did not understand — and told to sign. Then came an army camp, where recruits were trained in drone tactics, medical evacuation, and heavy weapons. When Rahman protested, a Russian commander replied through a translation app that his own agent had sent him there. Workers in his group were threatened with ten-year jail terms and beaten, he said.

His story is a case study in how this insidious war pipeline operates: a local agent, a borrowed fortune, a contract nobody could read, and a war that was never part of the bargain. But to understand how a man from Lakshmipur ended up in that camp, it’s important to look at the realities in Russia and what is driving these recruitment traps.
A war that is running out of men

Russia has a manpower problem, and the figures are hard to wave away. Enlistment into contract service dropped about 20 percent in the first quarter of 2026 compared with the same period a year earlier, according to international reporting relayed by Ukrainian outlets. This deficit persists even though Moscow is offering signing packages of up to USD 80,000 and debt write-offs of up to USD 140,000.

Meanwhile, BBC and Mediazona journalists estimate there have been at least 300,000 Russian deaths since the war began on February 24, 2022, based on local obituaries. Other Western intelligence estimates put Russian deaths near 500,000, with monthly casualties of 30,000 to 35,000.

One estimate says the country needs another 1.5 million workers to stabilize its labor market, and officials themselves expect a shortfall of 3.1 million people by 2030. Because stricter migration rules have also pushed out roughly a million temporary workers, the army and the factories now compete for the same shrinking labor pool.

While Russia has not dared to implement another full-scale military draft as it did in September 2022 — a move that was highly damaging to the regime and local support — officials are doing everything they can to buy recruits or force those who are vulnerable, elderly, or simply went to the draft station to register to go to the front lines.
Given these manpower challenges, Moscow has looked outward. It has already used tens of thousands of prisoners and three waves of North Korean troops, yet that wasn’t enough.

A UK defense assessment, summarized by a Ukrainian outlet, says the supply of convict recruits is probably exhausted, and Russia is widening its search across the Global South to avoid another mobilization at home.
Ukrainian data counts nearly 29,000 foreigners who have signed contracts since 2022. One report says the army wants at least 18,500 more in 2026, naming Bangladesh among its top targets.

Rights groups see a pattern behind these numbers. The International Federation for Human Rights described an organized pipeline aimed at undocumented migrants, detainees, precarious workers, and foreign students across three continents, and Amnesty International accused Moscow last month of deceptive, coercive, and exploitative recruitment.
Who is accepting this offer?

Within South Asia, this recruitment scheme goes beyond just Bangladesh. After Sri Lanka’s economic collapse in 2022 and Nepal’s recession, wages of at least USD 550 a month in Russia looked like a way out, according to analysis from the Observer Research Foundation (ORF). Nepal’s foreign minister admitted in early 2024 that more than 200 Nepali citizens had been recruited. Kathmandu later suspended work permits for Russia after numerous Nepali citizens died on the front lines in Ukraine. Sri Lanka, for its part, saw an estimated 600 to 700 former soldiers recruited.

Why, then, would anyone take the risk? Money comes first. One welder, according to a report on survivors’ accounts, was offered a USD 20,990 signing bonus, a salary of USD 2,664 per month, and a shot at citizenship. For families buried in debt, those numbers can drown out the danger.

But money isn’t the whole answer. Some Bangladeshis enlisted knowingly were misled about the role, the reporting noted, while others lost a visa-linked job and found a recruiter waiting with a better-sounding contract. Some never aimed for Russia at all: One prisoner said an Uzbek broker had promised him residence in Italy. Once inside, the choice largely disappears, as recruits were presented with contracts in Russian, with those who hesitated facing threats and violence, according to Fortify Rights and Truth Hounds. Another report described passports and phones seized on arrival.
The legal door and the missing agreement

Russia was never a typical destination for Bangladeshi workers. This labor force first entered the country via shipyards, where skilled hands were needed as the war strained the domestic labor supply. Initially, around 56 workers were sent there. Then the flow increased. According to the data of the Refugee and Migratory Movements Research Unit (RMMRU), 993 Bangladeshis went in 2024 and 4,663 in 2025. The Bureau of Manpower Employment and Training (BMET) records 8,247 departures between 2024 and June 2026. The state-run Bangladesh Overseas Employment and Services Limited (BOESL) sent just 426 among them, and those workers are reported safe; the private market carried the rest.

However, even with this sizable flow of workers, no signed labor agreement seems to exist between the two countries. During Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman’s June 2026 visit to Moscow, both sides merely urged early conclusion of pending accords, including a human resource agreement and a readmission agreement. Russia has agreed to fast-track a proposal for 100,000 Bangladeshi workers within a year. A state minister even spoke of 300,000 to 400,000 workers over five years. Meanwhile, Dhaka’s embassy in Moscow has asked Russia to bar Bangladeshis from military service.
The lack of a formal agreement leaves Bangladeshi workers exposed and vulnerable to scams and exploitation.
Fraud also shows up outside the war. In January 2026, 35 workers returned from Russia after being terminated, saying they had each paid about BDT 700,000 (roughly USD 5,651).
Agents, agencies, and the price of a seat

The route from village to barracks runs through ordinary offices. Bangladesh’s Special Response Battalion (SRB) said 30 men who flew to Russia in May 2026 went through three manpower firms, Jabal-e-Noor International, RS International, and TS Group. Officers arrested two alleged ringleaders in mid-October and say a Russian man and a Kyrgyz woman were part of the network, though these allegations remain unconfirmed. The expatriates’ welfare minister told Parliament that the men left with BMET clearance through licensed agencies, which shows that paperwork alone proves nothing.

Once the men landed, the script repeated. Their passports and phones were taken. After 21 days of training, they went to the front. Investigators said they were used as bait to expose enemy positions to drones.
Counting the dead without a count

Fortify Rights and Truth Hounds identified at least 104 Bangladeshis recruited as of February 2026 and at least 34 killed, based on Ukrainian information, and warned that the real toll is probably higher. But on October 14, 2026, the SRB said 20 of the same 30 were dead, with 17 killed by a drone strike on their first day at the front and six still fighting, local news reports said.
These figures can’t simply be added together, because the overlap is unknown and the sources differ: police, rights groups, and Kyiv. Those families, meanwhile, wait without bodies.

Rights groups have urged Dhaka to dismantle the networks and Ukraine to screen captured foreign fighters for signs of trafficking. Yet families still ask for rescue, and the same daily’s editors have pleaded with the government to start bringing the stranded men home.
No Justice for the victims

Back to Maksudur Rahman: He got out, and today he sits at home in Lakshmipur, holding up a Russian military dog tag as proof of where he has been. Others from the same corner of Bangladesh haven’t come home. Sajjad, 20, was killed after being taken to fight, and his father, Mohammed Siraj, now holds a photograph of where his son used to be. For Siraj, justice is not an abstraction. It is a name on a charge sheet, a body to bury, and an answer to the question of who sent his son to war.

In the village, families confronted the recruiting agents and demanded to know why their loved ones were being trained for war. Their questions belong in a courtroom, not only in a village courtyard. Until the agents who sold these jobs and the system that cleared their paperwork are made to answer, the families will keep carrying a debt that is more than money.
Rahman’s loan was real, the war was real, and the janitor’s job never existed. A man who left home to earn a living came back carrying a soldier’s dog tag. And no justice in sight.

articles.title: I study polling failures – this time, pollsters were mostly right, if not precise
articles.author: W Joseph Campbell, Professor Emeritus of Communication, American University School of Communication
paras: The crucial test for preelection polls is whether they broadly indicate how voters are likely to decide. By that fundamental measure, the 2026 midterm polls largely succeeded in anticipating outcomes on Election Day.
If somewhat tentatively, the polls overall had been signaling important gains for Democrats. And that is what voting produced.

It was, perhaps, polling’s most reassuring performance since accurately anticipating Barack Obama’s presidential election in 2008, an outcome cited in my book, “Lost in a Gallup: Polling Failure in U.S. Presidential Elections.”
This is not to say the 2026 preelection polls offered precision estimates before returns poured in. They appear to have underestimated support for Democratic candidates in some Senate races.

But spot-on precision, while enviable, is not what polls can be expected to produce, considering the many ways error can infiltrate opinion surveys. Given their checkered record in recent national elections, pollsters and media analysts tended to couch their end-of-campaign assessments in measured tentativeness.

For example, Nate Cohn, chief political analyst for The New York Times, wrote just before the election that “it’s reasonable to wonder whether the polls might be overestimating Democratic strength yet again. This is a real possibility. President Trump’s supporters are relatively unlikely to respond to polls, which introduces the ever-present risk of a polling misfire.”
That risk was mostly unrealized, as Republican candidates were swept in a red wipeout.
The 2026 polls tended to confirm the truism in American politics that midterms typically are rough on candidates of the party that holds the presidency.

Another truism, again reaffirmed, is that a president’s approval ratings often are useful in gauging the country’s mood before midterm elections. President Donald Trump’s preelection approval ratings hovered at or below 40%, according to survey data compiled by RealClearPolitics.
The U.S. war with Iran, launched by Trump, was a major factor propelling the unenviable ratings. The conflict went unresolved while fuel prices surged, bringing pain to consumers.

Those and other problems prompted polling analyst Nate Silver to write that Trump “almost seems to have a death wish in these midterms. And the one superpower he has – turning out low-propensity voters in presidential years, the sorts of voters who apparently are often missed by pollsters – has never really worked when Trump himself wasn’t on the ballot.”
And it didn’t work this time, either, even though throughout the campaign Trump encouraged supporters to pretend his name was on the ballot and turn out to vote.
When examined closely, the polls delivered some disagreement in the days before the election. Pollsters offered ranges that, in some races, were sizable.

For example, was Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton up by 1 percentage point in Texas late in the campaign, or was he down 7 points? Paxton lost by double digits to Democrat James Talarico, a margin that no pollster anticipated.

Similarly, was long-serving Republican Sen. Susan Collins ahead by 2 points in Maine or was she losing by 9 points? The outcome was closer to the latter reading, with Democrat Troy Jackson winning by more than six points.

In Minnesota, was Democratic Senate candidate Peggy Flanagan up by 14 points, or by just 2 points? With most votes counted by the day after the election, Flanagan’s margin of victory was about 10 points.
Such polling gaps in high-profile races offer a reminder to not focus on any single survey but, instead, to consider overall polling averages, which tend to remove or reduce the effects of outliers.

None of this necessarily is to declare that pollsters have resolved their persistent problems in sampling, especially in interviewing hard-to-reach voters. But big polling misses like that in the Texas governor’s race – where Democrat Gina Hinojosa won by double digits, although polls had shown Republican Gov. Greg Abbott ahead by a few points – were few this election cycle.
Meanwhile, the electorate’s broad inclinations were plainly if not precisely depicted.
That outcome has to be heartening for pollsters, an often-beleaguered and much-criticized cohort.

W Joseph Campbell does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Midterms are bad for incumbents – and even worse when energy prices are high
articles.author: Michael A. Mische, Associate Professor of the Practice of Management and Organization, Marshall School of Business, University of Southern California
paras: As Democrats and Republicans look at the overwhelming results of the 2026 midterm election, it’s worth remembering what has become a political axiom in America: “It’s the economy, stupid.” Democratic strategist James Carville famously said that to presidential candidate Bill Clinton in 1992, but he might have said “it’s energy prices” instead. The cost of energy underlies much of the economy, making energy and politics inseparable, especially when gasoline prices rise.
Midterm elections have historically been difficult for incumbent presidents and often shift the balance of power in Washington, D.C.

Many factors affecting gasoline prices are beyond a president’s or Congress’s control. Prices for crude oil and petroleum products such as gasoline are set on global markets as the results of economic forces of supply and demand. Even the companies that produce oil don’t have as much influence as people might think, because of how that oil gets to refineries: Over 60% of the world’s crude oil is transported by ocean tankers, with 20% of global supplies traveling through the Strait of Hormuz, which has been closed, or nearly so, for much of 2026 as the conflict with Iran drags on.
When energy prices rise, other prices, such as food, follow. Sudden spikes in gasoline prices can contribute to higher inflation, both regionally and nationally.

Voters pay attention to those changes, and incumbents are less likely to win reelection. For the 2026 midterm election, gasoline prices were the highest of any previous election. That put Republicans in the precarious position of defending their record.
Four American presidents – Gerald Ford, Jimmy Carter, Ronald Reagan and Joe Biden – confronted the consequences of severe inflation and high fuel prices during midterm elections.
Oil embargo, Nixon and Ford

Richard Nixon was the first modern president to truly face an energy crisis that became political. In retaliation for U.S. support for Israel during the October 1973 Yom Kippur War, Arab members of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries cut oil production and imposed an oil embargo on the United States. OPEC oil production fell by 5% a month, and crude oil prices rocketed 184% from prewar levels of $4.31 to $10.31 per barrel in March 1974. Nixon’s federal price controls on petroleum didn’t prevent U.S. gasoline prices from increasing 32%.
When Nixon resigned over the Watergate scandal in August 1974, Gerald Ford took office. Inflation was 12.3%, and gas prices were still high.
Right before that year’s midterm election, Ford launched the “Whip Inflation Now,” or WIN, campaign. But Republicans lost 48 House seats and five Senate seats.
“WIN” didn’t work, and by the 1976 presidential election, gas prices were over 60 cents a gallon – adjusted for inflation to late 2026, that’s $3.49. Ford lost his reelection bid to Jimmy Carter.
In Carter’s first two years in office, starting in 1977, the monthly average price of unleaded gasoline in the U.S. stayed high and even climbed slightly. Inflation hit 9% in 1978.

In the 1978 midterm election, Democrats lost 15 House and three Senate seats. Inflation continued to climb, and by the 1980 presidential election, gas prices were twice what they had been in 1976. Plagued by those figures and the Iranian hostage crisis, Carter lost the 1980 election to Ronald Reagan.

Reagan implemented “Reaganomics” by cutting taxes and regulations, reducing government spending, tightening monetary policy and removing the remaining price controls on petroleum. By the mid-1980s, increased oil production from U.S. and non-OPEC nations led to an oil glut, lowering the average price of crude oil and U.S. gasoline price from previous highs.
In the 1982 midterms, Republicans lost 26 seats in the House and gained one in the Senate.

Reagan won reelection to the presidency in a landslide in 1984, but the challenges for incumbents remained in the 1986 midterms. Though crude oil prices were $15 a barrel and gas had dropped to 82 cents a gallon, Republicans lost five seats in the House and eight in the Senate.

In the lead-up to the midterms during Donald Trump’s first term as president, crude prices had risen about 24% from when he took office in January 2017 to October 2018. And gas prices were up 22%. In the 2018 midterms, Republicans lost 41 House seats but gained two in the Senate.

Over the course of 2020, COVID-19 restrictions slowed the U.S. economy. U.S. crude oil production fell as gasoline demand plummeted by 40%. Prices rose because of pandemic-related supply chain backups.
And from Election Day in November 2020 to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the average price of unleaded gasoline in the U.S. rose by 66%, from $2.11 to $3.52 per gallon.
Also, as pandemic restrictions lifted and the economy began recovering, demand for gasoline rebounded, straining supplies.

Upon taking office in 2021, Biden took steps to curb rising energy costs, including releasing oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve in March 2022, which the Treasury Department suggested helped prevent gasoline price increases of $0.17 to $0.42 per gallon.

But other Biden policy moves made it harder to increase energy supplies. He canceled the Keystone XL pipeline project that would have brought more petroleum into the U.S. and suspended new oil and gas leases in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge and the Gulf of Mexico. He also recommitted the U.S. to the Paris climate accord, under which countries have promised to cut their greenhouse gas emissions, generally meaning moving away from fossil fuels as an energy source.
In June 2022, inflation reached 9.1%, a 40-year high. And U.S. gasoline prices reached an all-time high of $4.929 per gallon; adjusted for inflation, that’s $5.60 a gallon today.

The 2022 midterm election wasn’t as bad for Democrats as they might have feared, though it wasn’t a success: The party lost nine House seats and one Senate seat. That’s a reminder that energy prices aren’t the only factor in voters’ minds when they are casting ballots.

During the first 12 months of Trump’s second term, crude oil prices fell 4.5%, U.S. oil production rose 3.3%, from 13.3 million to 13.7 million barrels per day, and the AAA national average price of regular unleaded gasoline fell 4.5%, from $3.12 to $2.98 per gallon.

On Feb. 28, 2026, U.S. military action against Iran disrupted Middle Eastern oil production and oil tanker traffic in the Strait of Hormuz. Initially, shipment volume plummeted, though by the end of September it had recovered to 82% to 92% of prewar levels.

Overall, Middle Eastern crude oil exports are averaging around 24 million barrels a day, exceeding prewar levels in part because of increased use of pipelines out of Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. Because of the war with Iran, AAA’s national average price of unleaded regular gasoline has increased by almost 40%, from February’s $2.98 price to $4.15 a gallon as of Nov. 3, 2026.
As the preelection polling had suggested, voters held Trump accountable for high gasoline and grocery prices, as well as an unpopular war.

It was a reminder of a basic economic and political principle: When the economy is doing well, voters are more likely to support incumbents and their parties. And when voters are pessimistic about the economy’s future, they are inclined to vote against incumbents and their parties.

Michael A. Mische does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Blue wave: The Democrats’ historic midterm election gains could also offer Canada a path to peace
articles.author: Jason Opal, Professor of History, The Ohio State University
paras: During a CBC Radio interview yesterday, I predicted a good night for the Democrats in the United States midterm elections — with the possibility of a great one.

What happened was the biggest rout of an incumbent party since 2006, when the Iraq War doomed George W. Bush’s Republican Party. It might turn out to be an even bigger win, especially in the semi-tropical conservative heartland known as the Sun Belt, where the results seem like nothing less than a political revolution.

For Canadians, this is likely good news — with Democrats now in control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate, the historical friendship between the U.S. and Canada may return to a firmer footing. In at least one Senate race — in Maine, where longtime Republican incumbent Susan Collins was defeated by Democrat Troy Jackson — the Canada-U.S. trade war was a major campaign issue.
One former U.S. ambassador to Canada, Bruce Heyman, is already calling on Democrats to begin a reconciliation process with Canada.

In terms of what happened stateside, let’s start with Ohio, where I’ve lived since moving here from Montréal shortly before the 2024 presidential election. Donald Trump won Ohio by 11 points that year. A hotly contested battleground in the early 2000s, the Buckeye State, which has close economic ties with Canada, seemed safely Republican as recently as six months ago.

But last night, all the usual Democratic voters, including younger people, professionals, racialized people and many low-wage workers, turned out in droves. Independents and moderates broke for the Democrats, and conservative voters showed far less enthusiasm for Republican candidates than they had for Trump.

Take Lorain County, just west of Cleveland. A mostly white county of post-Second World War suburbs and poorer rural communities, Lorain went for the Democratic candidate for Senate, Sherrod Brown, by 11 points, just two years after favouring Trump by six.

Lorain broke for Dr. Amy Acton, the Democratic candidate for governor, by 14 percentage points — an extra jab, perhaps, at her Republican opponent, Trump acolyte Vivek Ramaswamy, who had run a brutal ad that questioned Acton’s honesty regarding the sexual abuse she suffered as a child.
In other traditional battlegrounds like Michigan and in newer “purple” states like North Carolina, the same story played out.

Democrats and independents flooded the polls, while Republicans stayed home or strayed from the party standard. Virtually every county shifted left relative to 2024, often by double digits, enabling the Democrats to take firm control of the U.S. Congress while also delivering governorships and state legislatures long held by Republicans.

The wide and deep character of the vote indicates a holistic rejection of Trump’s MAGA movement and his policies over the past two years, including the tariff war with Canada and other allies, the Iran war and the immigration crackdown. Voters also registered their disapproval of Republican efforts to redraw electoral districts and of Trump’s “let it ride” approach to AI development.
But the bigger story happened farther south, in states like South Carolina, Mississippi, Louisiana and, above all, Texas.

This huge band of rural poverty and suburban comfort — the Sun Belt — was once the place where cotton was king. It was a vast domain for a virulent strain of slavery that emerged in the early 1800s and refused to remain in the same country as Abraham Lincoln and his “Black Republicans” (the Republicans, founded in the mid-1850s, included abolitionists and pledged to contain slavery).

After the Civil Rights movement of the 1950s and ‘60s, these states shifted dramatically to the right, embracing the Republicans as the party of small government, evangelical piety and proud patriotism. Mostly white Republicans have simply overwhelmed the majority Black and Democratic strongholds of their states.
In 2026, however, historically Black counties in places like the Mississippi Delta turned out in such huge numbers that the weakened Republican vote could no longer hold.
As of this writing, the Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate, Scott Colom, is leading the incumbent Republican by 43 votes out of nearly 950,000 cast.

And then there is the biggest prize of all: Texas, one of only a handful of U.S. states that was once an independent republic, in this case a slaveholders’ cotton-growing frontier called the Lone Star Republic (1836-46).

Home to more than 31 million people, Texas is not shy about being Texas. (My grandfather, a Second World War veteran, proudly told me that he once got into a fist fight with his Texas-born superior when that officer tried to make my grandfather stand and sing, “The Yellow Rose of Texas.”)
Around 40 per cent of Texans are Spanish-speaking voters who generally prefer Democrats but who had veered towards Trump two years ago.
For example, Webb County — on the border with Mexico — had gone to Trump in 2024 by two points. Last night, the Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate, James Talarico, won it by 47 points.
I repeat: A county moved nearly 50 points in two years.
What happens now depends on whether the Democrats can consolidate last night’s mighty alliance of moderates, young people, racialized people, professionals and lower wage earners.
To do so, they will have to drop their occasional aversion to piety in public life (Talarico is a devout Presbyterian who gave his victory speech in front of the words “Love Thy Neighbor.”)
They will need to address economic problems. They will need to be disciplined.

If they can do so, then the entire political map of the U.S. will be transformed, with the Sun Belt coloured purple and the Democratic Party capable of the kind of sustained dominance we haven’t seen since Ronald Reagan’s Republicans in the 1980s.
As Canadians have learned over the last two years, and more broadly over the last two centuries, America can always surprise you.
Jason Opal has received funding from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada.

articles.title: We used ancient DNA to track the origins and spread of the Germanic and Celtic languages – new research
articles.author: Guus Kroonen, Associate Professor,  Scandinavian, Germanic and Indo-European Comparative Linguistics, Leiden University; University of Copenhagen
paras: Why do people speak Germanic languages such as English in England and Swedish in Sweden, but Celtic languages in Ireland, Wales and Brittany? The dispersal of languages is one of the enigmas of European prehistory.
Two new studies in Nature, which we took part in, show how DNA from several thousand ancient individuals helps us solve this riddle.

As early as the 17th century, scholars noticed striking similarities between the European languages. English father, Swedish fader, Irish athair, Latin pater and Greek patḗr do not resemble each other by coincidence. Today, we know that these languages, together with Baltic, Slavic, Indic and Iranian, evolved from a common ancestor: Proto-Indo-European.

But how did this ancestral language come to be spoken so widely across Eurasia? During the 19th and 20th centuries, a wide variety of theories were developed about its origin. One of these placed its homeland on the vast grassy steppes north of the Black and Caspian Seas around 5,000 years ago.
Subsequent migrations by the pastoral nomads of the Yamnaya culture are thought to have spread the ancestral language across Europe and Asia.

The occurrence of such a migration, inferred from archaeology, was debated for over a century with the answer seemingly lost to time. However, thanks to ancient DNA, we now know that large groups of people migrated from the Eastern European steppes to Europe around 5,000 years ago, providing compelling support for the spread of Indo-European languages from that region.

Today, the spread of Indo-European languages from the steppes is accepted by most historical linguists. Yet several questions remain: how did the individual Indo-European languages subsequently spread to their historically known locations?

As part of an international collaboration, led by researchers from the University of Copenhagen in Denmark and Leiden University in the Netherlands, we analysed the DNA of thousands of prehistoric Europeans, including more than 700 newly sequenced individuals. This allowed us to test, for the first time, specific theories on the prehistoric dispersals of the Germanic and Celtic languages.
The first Germanic speakers in Northern Europe?

It has long been assumed that the earliest form of Germanic arrived in Scandinavia with the first steppe migrants around 4,800 years ago. This event would then have been followed by several millennia of linguistic and genetic continuity.
Our analyses yielded a surprisingly different result. Around 4,000 years ago, a second group with steppe ancestry appeared in Eastern Scandinavia, probably arriving from across the Baltic Sea.

This previously unknown population spread across much of Scandinavia, ultimately matching the region where the ancestral form of Germanic is believed to have been spoken during the first millennium BC.

This distribution, combined with their ancestry persisting in most later Germanic-speaking populations, suggests these newcomers may have introduced the precursor of the Germanic languages, some 800 years later than traditionally assumed. In this scenario, the timeline for the language history of Northern Europe is reset.
Anglo-Saxons and Vikings share a surprising past

Our understanding of the regions where specific Germanic languages were spoken suddenly comes into focus around 2,000 years ago. At this point, writing spread to northern Europe in the form of the runic alphabet, allowing us to compare migrations with the spread of the Germanic languages we still know today.

By around 2,000 years ago, people from Scandinavia began spreading south, into present-day Poland, Germany and the Netherlands. During the Migration Period, beginning around 400 AD, related populations from around northern Germany subsequently dispersed across Europe. Among them were the West Germanic-speaking Anglo-Saxons, who settled in England and the Langobards, who ultimately established a kingdom in Italy.

But we also discovered a migration in the opposite direction. People from northern Germany and southern Jutland, still largely descending from Eastern Scandinavians, moved back into Denmark and southern Sweden. Intriguingly, they were closely related to the ancestors of the Anglo-Saxons who migrated to England, which may help explain similar art styles and cultural elements between the regions.

This migration coincided with major cultural changes in Southern Scandinavia, the emergence of new political centers and the earliest stages in the development of Old Norse, the language of the Vikings.
Norway, however, tells a different story. Despite remaining largely unaffected by this migration, pre-Viking Age Norwegians still participated in the linguistic changes that gave rise to Old Norse.
This suggests that linguistic changes spread not only through migration, but also through cultural contact between closely related Scandinavian communities.
A new perspective on the origins of Celtic

Before the spread of Germanic and the expansion of the Roman Empire, Celtic languages were spoken across much of Europe, from Spain and France to southern Germany and the Balkans. Today, they survive mainly along the Atlantic coast, particularly in Ireland, Wales and Brittany.

The origins of the Celtic languages have also long been debated. Some scholars propose that they emerged along the Atlantic and subsequently spread eastwards. Others place their origins in Central Europe, in the context of the Bronze Age Urnfield and successive Iron Age Hallstatt and La Tène cultures.

Our genetic analyses provide the strongest support for the latter scenario. Between 3,200 and 2,800 years ago, ancestry associated with populations of the Urnfield culture expanded westward into France and Great Britain, eventually reaching northeastern Spain. This closely matches the model for the spread of Celtic from central Europe.

However, an earlier Atlantic migration from southwestern Europe into Britain, around 3,800 years ago, offers partial support for theories proposing western Celtic origins, indicating the process was potentially more complex.

Ancient DNA cannot reveal the language or languages a particular individual spoke. But by comparing prehistoric population movements with archaeological and linguistic evidence, we can increasingly test competing theories about how languages spread.

Our studies reveal a complex European past in which populations, cultures and languages develop through repeated migrations, contact and mixture. Thanks to ancient DNA, we can now reconstruct that history with unprecedented precision.
