articles.title: Donald Trump’s Republicans suffer landslide defeat – what this means for the world
articles.author: Andrew Gawthorpe, Lecturer in History and International Studies, Leiden University
paras: Donald Trump’s Republican Party has received a stunning rebuke in the US midterm elections. Republicans went into the evening hoping that the polls might be wrong and that they could at least cling on to control of the Senate. But by midnight in Washington, the GOP was staring down what looked like its worst defeat in 50 years.

Republican losses were not just confined to the type of swing districts that parties usually worry about on election night. The scale of the losses was staggering. They lost Senate seats in deep red states such as Texas and South Carolina. They lost districts they had gerrymandered and in which they were supposed to be unbeatable. They lost seats that even the sharpest analysts thought were safe.

Why? For months, surveys have shown that voters are fed up with high prices, with the war in Iran, and with what is increasingly being talked about as the Trump administration’s corruption. A president who was narrowly elected on the promise of a steady economic hand instead spent two years pursuing an extreme ideological agenda favoured only by a minority of Americans. He ignored what voters were saying, and now they have delivered a harsh verdict.

But these results have implications beyond just the remainder of Trump’s presidency. They break some of the patterns that have defined American politics for decades. Democrats are suddenly winning in places where they have been counted out for a generation. Suddenly, the American political map looks different.

Take Texas. The last time a Democrat won election as a senator there was 1988. Democrats have not won a presidential election in Texas since Jimmy Carter in 1976. Yet last night, Democrat James Talarico powered to a convincing victory. If elections in Texas become politically competitive on a permanent basis, it will become much harder for Republicans to take the presidency in the future.

The Republican Party will now be looking nervously towards the 2028 election. For the first time since 2016, there is likely to be a serious debate within the party about whether to move on from the aggressive nationalism and bigotry of Trump’s “Make America Great Again” movement. Democrats, meanwhile, face their own questions about how to capitalise on their victories.

But for the rest of the world, change might not come so quickly. Despite the fact that his party has suffered this electoral setback, Trump remains president until 2028. And because despite its constitutional role in declaring war and ratifying treaties, Congress tends to be less involved in foreign policy, there is still a lot that he can do with that power.

Indeed, US presidents whose parties perform badly in midterm elections often become more active in foreign policy than they had previously. With the chance of passing a significant domestic agenda mostly beyond their reach, they have a more time on their hands to think about America’s relations with the rest of the world. The same is likely to be true of Trump.

The fact that the midterms are over also means that Trump no longer has to be so careful about the political consequences of his actions. As the midterm elections got closer, the president has backed down from major military confrontation with Iran and sought a truce in his tariff wars. Now, with political constraints lifted, he could become more erratic and unpredictable.

Congress would not be completely powerless to stop him, at least in theory. But most actions it can take – such as cutting off funding for the war with Iran or seizing tariff power back from the president – require margins of control in both chambers that Democrats are unlikely to have, despite their formidable victories.

They would need to have a two-thirds majority to override an almost certain presidential veto on any attempt to pass laws to achieve these outcomes. So a key question is whether this midterm drubbing was serious enough to make some Republican members of Congress get serious about joining Democrats in restraining Trump.

Something that Democrats will definitely be able to do is launch all manner of investigations into the conduct of the Trump administration and some of its officials. Their efforts are likely to focus on the war with Iran, Trump’s personal financial dealings with foreign leaders, and the management of the Pentagon by secretary of defence Pete Hegseth.
Hegseth, indeed, could be an early casualty of these efforts – there is speculation that he will resign or be fired rather than face possible impeachment.

But ultimately a change of direction in US foreign policy depends on the decisions of Trump himself. A changing of the guard among his advisers, or in Congress, can only do so much to influence a president who has never willingly submitted to constraint.
The world should prepare itself for the possibility that a politically wounded and angry Trump could now decide to vent his frustrations abroad.
Andrew Gawthorpe is a senior fellow at the Foreign Policy Centre in London.

articles.title: Egypt’s crackdown on independent media reaches Mada Masr as editor faces trial
articles.author: Walid El Houri
paras: Egypt convicted Mada Masr’s Lina Attalah in a hearing marred by violations, and ordered it closed
Originally published on Global Voices
Lina Attalah. Photo from Mada Masr website, used with permission.
A crackdown on independent media in Egypt is escalating.

The latest wave of suppression of the country’s last remaining critical voices began with the violent arrest of the entire newsroom of Matsada2sh, a fact-checking and open-source intelligence (OSINT) page that relies on social media and is run by young journalists.

The six-person team was forcibly disappeared, illegally detained, and interrogated under torture for several days before being charged with terrorism and spreading false news. They remain in pretrial detention.

The crackdown then reached Mada Masr, one of Egypt’s most prominent independent outlets, and its founder and editor-in-chief, Lina Attalah. On November 11, Attalah is due to stand trial for the second time in two weeks, this time on charges of spreading false news that carry a possible prison sentence.

The new trial follows her conviction on October 27, when a court found her guilty of managing a news website without a license, in a single hearing marred by violations of her right to a fair trial. She was given the maximum fine of EGP 3 million (about USD 55,000) and was forcibly removed from the courtroom and held until the fine was paid, seven hours later. The court also ordered Mada Masr shut down and all of its equipment confiscated.

According to Mada Masr, the judge appointed a lawyer to represent Attalah even though eight of her own lawyers were in the courtroom and she objected. The outlet says her objection was not recorded in the session’s minutes.
Amnesty International reports that Mada Masr applied for a license from the Supreme Council for Media Regulation in 2018 and 2020 and received no response, and submitted a new application in 2026.

Mada Masr was founded in 2013 as an independent, critical, investigative outlet. In another decade of operation, Mada Masr was instrumental in informing the public about what is happening in Egypt, as well as in the region. It gave a platform to torture victims and the families of political prisoners, and created space for debate on reproductive rights.

Its reporting on the genocides in Sudan and Gaza uncovered abuses and stood with refugees facing xenophobic attacks and security crackdowns. The outlet has also long engaged with technology issues and advocated for a free, independent internet for the global majority.
The attack comes at a crucial point in Egypt’s and the region’s history, and goes beyond a question of human rights or activism. At least 25 journalists are currently imprisoned in Egypt.

On Friday, October 30, Mada Masr published a statement on Instagram describing an “ongoing battle” and its efforts at “finding a legal way to continue [its] work while also taking care of each other in this moment of madness.” A wave of solidarity has mobilized supporters in Egypt and abroad.

“This is the kind of social movement, the doing of politics, how a newsroom is connected to its community, that we in our everyday practice would want to write about. But this time it is us whom it was happening to,” the statement reads. It concludes: “We are angry but hopeful, we are tired but insistent that our work must go on, that Lina should face neither prison nor fines, that all jailed journalists should be free.”

A joint statement led by Amnesty International and signed by organizations worldwide condemned “in the strongest terms the conviction of Lina Attalah, and the court’s order to shut down one of the country’s leading and last remaining independent newsrooms.” It called on Egyptian authorities to allow Mada Masr to operate freely.

In an op-ed published on October 26, the Mada Masr team wrote that “in this ongoingness of normalcy and crisis, perhaps a feature of our world today, but also a mastery we have mastered in the region, in learning to live in the world with the genocide on Gaza, we will go to court on Tuesday while continuing to publish Sunday through Saturday.”

They added: “There is something psychically bordering on horror when you see your own image as a journalist, instead of your journalism, surfacing on repeat through the scrolling movement of the Internet. But, in a moment like this, there is no tomorrow without solidarity and journalism.”

And: “We are reassured, once more, that the journalism we do is not for itself. And together with the few independent voices wrestling with sense-making and truth-snatching in a world where power condescendingly tells us to give up, this is not just about a small us, Mada Masr, but a much bigger we.”

In Egypt, journalists who documented torture, political imprisonment, and security crackdowns now face courts that process them quickly and unfairly, under a licensing scheme that has left applicants without an answer for years.
For journalism to be free, that licensing scheme and its chilling effects on access to information, knowledge production, and critical voices in Egypt and beyond must be stopped.

articles.title: Unpacking Hong Kong’s rule of law score according to the World Justice Project’s ranking
articles.author: Oiwan Lam
paras: Hong Kong ranks 24th in rule of law index and is trending down
Originally published on Global Voices
Screenshot from the World Justice Project's Rule of Law Index. Fair use.

This post is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here.

The Hong Kong anti-graft body, the Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC), flaunted on X in early October that the city ranked in the top 10 globally and third in Asia in the “Absence of Corruption” category on the “Rule of Law Index 2026” published by the World Justice Project (WJP).

However, the “Absence of Corruption” merely captures whether or not public officials from the administration, police force, and judiciary use their offices for private gain; this single factor does not mean a society is free from corruption, as institutional favoritism, such as political nepotism, legal discrimination, and cronyism, are equally dangerous abuses of power that create systematic injustice. That’s why the WJP includes eight major factors in its index, and Hong Kong ranks 24th and scored 0.71 in the overall index among 143 countries, falling behind Australia (12), Singapore (14), Japan (15), and South Korea (20) in Asia and the Pacific. Between 2016 and 2020, Hong Kong consistently ranked 16th overall in the index.

The eight factors considered in the Rule of Law Index are “constraints on government power,” “absence of corruption,” “open government,” “fundamental rights,” “order and security,” “regulatory enforcement,” “civil justice,” and “criminal justice.”
Best performance: “order and security” and “absence of corruption”

Hong Kong performs best in “order and security” (ranked seventh with a 0.92 score), “absence of corruption” (ranked 10th with a 0.83 score), and “regulatory enforcement (ranked 16th with a 0.79 score). Among the subfactors of “order and security,” the city indeed has a relatively low crime rate (ranked eighth), and near-zero violent expression of grievance (ranked ninth).

In fact, the city has had hardly any protests since 2021, following the enactment of the National Security Law on June 30, 2020, and a heavy-handed crackdown on unauthorized protests. However, civic conflict remains high (ranked 40th), as people resort to street fights to express their frustrations.

The average Hongkonger will likely disagree with the relatively high ranking of “regulatory enforcement,” particularly after the recent release of the Taipo Deadly Fire investigation report, which revealed that multiple Hong Kong government authorities, including the Housing Bureau, the Labor Department, the Fire Service Department, and the Buildings Department, had not effectively enforced related regulations, which could have prevented the death of 168 individuals on November 25, 2025.

Moreover, while Hongkongers have complained about tender rigging in building renovations for over a decade, it was only after the high-profile Taipo fire that the authorities vowed to actively investigate the construction sector. Some fire victims also criticized the government’s buy-back plan as disrespectful of their private property rights. Both effectiveness of regulatory enforcement and respecting property rights are subfactors of “regulatory enforcement” in the Index.
Worst performance: “constraints in government's power” and “fundamental rights”
Hong Kong’s worst performance among the eight categories is “constraints in government’s power” (ranked 63rd with a 0.54 score) and “fundamental rights” (ranked 69th with a 0.55 score).

Hong Kong ranked 25th in “constraints in government’s power” in 2016, fell to 31st in 2020, then plummeted to 54th in 2022, and further tumbled to 63rd in 2025 and 2026. The enactment of the National Security Law in Hong Kong on June 30, 2020, which empowered the Hong Kong government to shut down independent media outlets and NGOs, was the main driving force in the recent plunges. Other factors included officials’ decision to rewrite electoral laws under the guiding principle of “patriots administering Hong Kong” in May 2021, the 2023 district council reform to restrict district councilors’ power and exclude oppositional figures, and the passage of domestic security law in March 2024 to outlaw acts including treason, espionage that harms the city, and incitement that provokes hatred. Rights groups say all of these provisions have chilled civil society activity and encroached on citizens’ fundamental rights.

The report described the “constraints in government’s power” performance as moderately to alarmingly risky, with constraints from the legislature ranking 84, judiciary 64, independent auditing and review bodies 61, non-government organizations 105, and the law 90 — the law refers to the legal framework that protects procedural justice and integrity regarding the appointment of officials and the electoral process. As for the subfactor “official sanctioned for misconduct,” which has a fair 22 ranking, some Hongkongers may consider the score too generous given that only one official has taken responsibility and resigned over the preventable Taipo Fire disaster.

A similar downward trend appears in the “fundamental rights” category, which ranked 29th in 2015, slipped to 38th in 2020, plummeted to 54th in 2021, and fell to 69th in 2026. The at-risk subfactors include security of suspects and dissidents (73), freedom of opinion and expression (105), privacy protection (86), freedom of assembly and association (115), and labor rights (66).

Hong Kong saw the shutdown of Apple Daily News and Stand News in 2021 upon the enactment of the National Security Law in 2020. The domestic Article 23 security law was enacted in March 2024 to further clamp down on “soft resistance” with the newly introduced sedition crime. Privacy rights have declined, as implementation rules for national security laws have empowered police to conduct physical searches of private property and digital devices without court warrants during national security investigations. Since 2020, NGOs, independent media outlets, and activist groups have vanished en masse amid a tightening political environment and shrinking civic space for organizational activities.
The fairly ranked subfactors are freedom from discrimination (29), rights of the accused and convicted (32), and freedom of religion (31).
Poor performance on “fundamental rights” also drags down the “open government” factor's rank (29), with its subfactor “civic participation” ranking 87 in an at-risk level.
Downgraded “civil justice” and “criminal justice”
Although Hong Kong's overall performance in civil and criminal justice remains fair, both factors have fallen from their historical high ranks of 11th and 7th to the current 20th and 23rd.
The main subfactors driving the decline in civil justice are discrimination (48) and improper government influence (56).

After the passage of Legal Aid Reforms in 2021, the number of applications to fund judicial review that challenge the government’s policy and decisions received by the Legal Aid Department dropped 60 percent from around 275 in 2016 to 110 in 2025. Of those 110 requests, the department approved only 2 cases. The overall number of judicial review cases fell from a peak of 3,899 in 2019 to 1,545 in 2022. Because most cases involve non-refoulement claims for refugee status, the government, in addition to the administrative Unified Screening Mechanism (USM) launched in 2014, introduced a special scheme in March 2025 to appoint eligible private practitioners as Deputy Judges of the Court of First Instance to handle these cases exclusively. The mechanism disposed of more than 3700 claims in 2025. Both reforms, driven by the government administration's political considerations, have negatively affected the poor and the non-citizen's access to judicial justice in Hong Kong.
The major subfactor contributing to the fall in criminal justice ranking is “government or political influence on the criminal justice system” (61).

Hong Kong’s criminal justice ranking first plunged in 2017, from 8th to 16th, after the government labeled the civil unrest in Mong Kok, dubbed the Fishball Revolution, as a riot and reactivated the colonial-era Public Order Ordinance to prosecute protesters en masse. Then, in 2021 and 2022, the ranking dropped again amid a series of speech-related national security prosecutions against 47 pro-democracy activists for participating in the primaries of the election of the legislature for conspiracy to subvert, Apple Daily senior executives for foreign collusion, and Stand News editors for conspiracy to publish seditious content. The recent convictions and heavy sentencing of Apple Daily’s executives, including Jimmy Lai, and former leaders over collusion, Albert Ho Chun-yan, Lee Chuek-yan and Chow Hang-tung, of the now-disbanded organizer of the June 4th candlelight vigil, Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China, over inciting subversion, may further downgrade the city’s criminal justice performance in the next year. The fact that all these controversial cases were handled by judges designated by the Chief Executive adds weight to the evaluation of “government or political influence on the criminal justice system”.

According to the Index’s insights, the global rule of law has declined for 9 consecutive years. Civic participation and the freedoms of speech and assembly each fell in over 60 percent of countries, and Hong Kong is among them. The city also sees the global trend of improper government influence that undermines civil and criminal justice.

The Rule of Law Index is particularly crucial to global financial centers; as the WJP notes, when the index scores reach 0.66, countries tend to have high sovereign credit ratings. Currently, Hong Kong’s score is 0.71 and trending down, while its Asian competitor, Singapore, ranks 14th with a 0.79 score and an upward trend. Watchdogs indicate this could be a bad sign for the city as it seeks to secure its spot as the region’s top economy.

articles.title: Can democracy be taught? Brazil is about to find out
articles.author: Gabriel Marmentini, Policy Leader Fellow at the Florence School of Transnational Governance, European University Institute
paras: Brazil’s experience offers lessons for other democracies, including Europe, that are turning to education to strengthen democratic resilience.
Knowing how institutions work is not enough: democracy is learned through experience as much as via content.
Civic education mandates often fail between the law and the classroom. Teachers, time and democratic school life decide whether they take hold.

In Brazil’s presidential run-off on October 25, President Lula turned the result around against the odds by winning a fourth term with 51.77% of the valid votes. It was the first time since Brazil’s return to democracy that the runner-up in the first round went on to win.
First-round abstention reached 21.08 %, the highest rate in a presidential election since 1998. It fell to 19.22% in the run-off, but more than 30 million eligible voters still stayed away.

This is no one-off: abstention has crept up since 2006, when it stood at 16.75%. Experts blame disenchantment after decades of scandals and two presidential impeachments, voters registered in towns they have left, and fines up to R$3.51, less than one euro, for those who neither vote nor justify their absence. In a country where voting is compulsory for most adults, seeing it as a right, rather than merely a duty, will require a deeper cultural shift.

That shift begins long before election day, through civic education : learning not only how democracy works, but how to question, act and influence public life by tackling concrete problems in their communities.

Yet civic education received little attention in the campaign. In his platform, Lula proposed a national digital literacy policy to combat disinformation. The policy would teach people of all ages, especially older people, to navigate the internet critically, but the programme says little about schools. Flávio Bolsonaro, for his part, pledged schools that teach students “how to think, not what to think”, free from partisan indoctrination, and more civic-military schools.
Beyond electoral promises, what is Brazil’s long-term vision for preparing citizens to take part in democracy?

Brazil’s 1988 Federal Constitution already states that education must prepare people for the exercise of citizenship. The 1996 National Education Guidelines and Bases Law (LDB) made this one of the core aims of basic education, and the National Common Core Curriculum (BNCC) includes citizenship among the skills every student should develop.

Yet the gaps are large. The 2022 International Civic and Citizenship Education Study (ICCS) found significant gaps in Brazilian students’ civic knowledge. According to the OECD’s 2024 Truth Quest Survey, Brazilians had the lowest ability among 21 countries to distinguish between true and false or misleading online content, with an accuracy rate of 54%, compared to an average of 60%.

In September 2025, the executive branch responded: a ministerial ordinance created the Brazilian Ministry of Education’s Programme for Citizenship and Sustainability Education. Joining is voluntary, yet by July 2026 all but one of Brazil’s 26 states and 57% of its municipalities had signed up.
Its competency matrix sets out 46 skills, from pre-school to the end of secondary school, in three strands :
fundamental rights and environmental citizenship
the democratic ecosystem and its defence

Pupils should learn, for example, to recognise democratic breakdowns and authoritarian proposals in Brazil’s history, to understand what the Supreme Court and the leaders of both houses of Congress do, to tell free speech from hate speech, and to take part in their school’s democratic bodies, such as student councils.

Networks that join must appoint a coordinator and draw up a local plan, and teachers can take online courses on the ministry’s platform. The programme’s own guide acknowledges “significant gaps” in citizenship education in Brazil, and promises a national plan to monitor implementation and learning outcomes.
In July 2026, more than a decade after the original bill was introduced, a new law amended the LDB to make civic education a compulsory curricular component.

It is not the first time. In 1969, the military junta made moral and civic education compulsory at every level, alongside a secondary-school subject called Brazilian Social and Political Organisation (OSPB). Among its stated aims was “the cult of the homeland, its symbols, traditions and institutions”. After the return to democracy, a 1993 law abolished both and folded their content into the humanities. Civic education is therefore, not new to Brazil.
The challenge is to understand what each curriculum really sets out to teach.

The new law has an unusual cross-party history. It was signed under Lula’s government, but originated in a bill by federal deputy Renata Abreu, leader of Podemos, a party that formally backed Flávio Bolsonaro in the run-off.
In a deeply polarised country, could civic education become a rare point of common ground?

Its reach will also depend on how the law and the programme fit together, since one is compulsory and the other is voluntary. Ideally, each feeds the other: the law gives the 43% of municipalities still outside the programme in July a reason to join, and the programme gives schools the means to comply. Together, they could take civic education to every school; apart, many schools will face a new duty without the means to meet it.

The law makes civic education compulsory, but not necessarily as a standalone subject. It could be woven into existing classes, such as history, geography and Portuguese, or taught through interdisciplinary projects. Given the autonomy of Brazil’s education systems, some states could also make it a separate subject.

Much remains to be defined. The law does not specify teaching hours, grade levels, teacher qualifications or materials. Its incorporation into the National Common Core Curriculum still requires approval by the National Education Council and ratification by the education minister. Only then will states, municipalities and schools adapt their curricula.

In October, the electoral court and the education ministry agreed to work together on regulation, teaching materials and school election simulations. Learning by doing has a track record: since 2004, the Chamber of Deputies’ Youth Parliament has brought 78 secondary school students to Brasília for each edition, to debate and vote on bills as if they were deputies. But such programmes reach few pupils, and institutional commitment is only a first step.

Nor is the new law consensual. Associations of philosophy and social science teachers asked for a veto, fearing it would weaken philosophy and sociology, and the Escola sem Partido movement warned of ideological indoctrination. Though raised from different angles, both concerns point to the same condition for success: teachers trained not only in content, but in a professional ethic above party lines, so that students learn to form their own views rather than adopt someone else’s.

Brazilians even have an expression for laws that never take hold: “Leis que não pegam.” This gap is precisely why Politize !, the non-partisan civic education institute I co-founded in 2015, has run its Active Citizenship School programme for over eight years. In Brazilian public schools alone, more than 19,000 teachers have used its training and materials to reach around 288,000 students. In 2026, this work earned Politize! the European Union’s Human Rights Award in Brazil.

For the new law to take hold, civic education must be cross-curricular but with clear owners, interdisciplinary but not diluted, and non-partisan but not depoliticised. It will need teacher training, suitable materials, curricular time, coordination and monitoring.
Could this law become the opportunity to bring civic education to scale across Brazil?
When democracies turn to the classroom

Brazil would not be the first country to turn to the classroom when its political order is under strain. In such moments, civic education is less an education policy than an attempt to rebuild a shared democratic project.

In 1952, a West Germany rebuilding after Nazism and war created a federal agency to consolidate and spread democratic and European ideas among Germans, today’s Federal Agency for Civic Education. In 1976, a meeting of educators from across the political spectrum gave rise to the Beutelsbach Consensus : teachers must not indoctrinate, must present contested issues as contested, and must enable students to take part in democracy. Fifty years on, it remains the standard in German classrooms, and a useful reference for Brazil’s own fears of indoctrination.

Latin America offers closer parallels. In Chile, after a wave of corruption scandals, a 2016 law required every state-recognised school to adopt a citizenship education plan and paved the way for a compulsory subject, Citizenship Education, in the final two years of secondary school, which was introduced in 2020. In Colombia, a 2014 law passed during peace talks with the FARC guerrillas made a course on the culture of peace compulsory in every school and a 2015 decree required it to be assessed in the national school-leaving exam.

Other countries have focused on participation. In Argentina, a 2013 law requires education authorities to recognise and support student councils in secondary schools. In Mexico, the electoral authority, INE, gives children and teenagers the opportunity to vote on issues that affect them: more than 10 million people aged 3 to 17 took part in 2024.

Across Latin America, civic education often stops at declarations. A 2020 UNESCO review of primary-school curricula in 19 countries in the region (Brazil’s included) found that citizenship features in all of them, but that such concepts appear more often in statements of principle than in the content teachers use to plan lessons.

Europe shows that a place in the curriculum is only half the battle. Italy, for instance, made civic education compulsory in 2019 as a cross-curricular subject of at least 33 hours a year, shared among each class’ teachers and taught since 2020.

Across Europe, the weak link has been teacher preparation. When the EU’s Eurydice network reviewed 42 education systems in 2017, 17 had no central rules or recommendations on preparing future teachers for citizenship education, and only 13 of the 36 systems that taught it across subjects defined what all future secondary teachers should master.

A new Eurydice report, due in December, will show what has changed and give Brazil and its neighbours a benchmark. In the end, teachers decide whether civic education takes hold, and they can only do so if education systems prepare and support them.

Brazil’s run-off showed what is at stake. Citing transport failures and floods, Supreme Court justice Cristiano Zanin extended voting by two hours nationwide, after both campaigns had requested extensions in some areas. Flávio Bolsonaro called the decision unacceptable, refused to concede and said he would seek to annul the election. Whether the decision was right is for institutions to judge.

Within days, after Supreme Court justice Alexandre de Moraes ordered him to surrender his passports in a money-laundering investigation, Flávio Bolsonaro left Brazil for the United States. His allies called it political exile from judicial persecution. Critics, Lula among them, replied that “those with nothing to hide have nothing to fear”, and some suggested he was getting ahead of January, when his Senate term ends, and with it the special legal standing it grants. Each side tells a ready-made story.
When politics works more like a clash of tribes, or a form of entertainment, than a shared civic space, no school subject can protect citizens on its own.

What civic education can offer is a shared grammar for such decisive moments on the political agenda: separating facts from narratives, accepting results, and contesting electoral proceedings and practices through evidence, transparency and the courts.
Lula’s new term will be the first to implement the law that seeks to promote civic education. Making it work will require treating civic education as state policy, not government policy.

Brazil already obliges its citizens to vote; the harder task is preparing them to vote well and to take part in democracy between elections. If the law succeeds, the country will have shown the many democracies now turning to the classroom that democracy can be taught and, above all, practised.

articles.title: How North Korea became a world leader in state-sponsored hacking
articles.author: Jinkyung Baek, PhD Candidate in Politics Research, King's College London
paras: Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, was the victim of a massive heist in late October. Approximately US$6.36 billion (£4.74 billion) of funds were stolen within the space of 20 minutes in an attack that has been described as the largest of its kind in history.

The source of the attack has not yet been officially confirmed. But the FBI and blockchain analytics company TRM Labs identified North Korea’s TraderTraitor hacking unit as the group most likely to have been behind it. Two other blockchain analytics firms, Chainalysis and Elliptic, have supported this attribution.

This is not the first time North Korea has been linked to cyber-attacks. Several other cryptocurrency exchange thefts in recent years have been attributed to North Korean state-sponsored hackers. These include the 2019 Upbit and 2025 Bybit hacks, where funds worth US$42 million and US$1.5 billion respectively were stolen.

Therefore, while Pyongyang has always denied any involvement in state-sponsored cyber warfare, it is not surprising that North Korea has once again been mentioned in connection with a major crypto heist.

North Korea’s cyber operations are the product of decades of strategic development. The North Korean state began building the technological foundations for these operations in the 1980s, establishing domestic computing infrastructure, specialised educational institutions and state-led research centres.

The development of its cyber capabilities intensified in the 1990s. The Korea Computer Center was set up in 1990 to oversee national IT development. And in 1995, North Korea’s then-leader, Kim Jong-il, directed the military to develop cyber capabilities as a strategic component of national defence.
IT education was further institutionalised from 1998 onward after computer education was made compulsory for all students from the fourth year of middle school.

North Korea began conducting major cyber-attacks in the 2000s. Early operations primarily targeted South Korea. But its cyber operations gradually expanded beyond the Korean peninsula, with the 2017 WannaCry attack a prominent example of this development.

This attack targeted computers running the Microsoft Windows operating system and demanded ransom payments in the form of bitcoin cryptocurrency. It was estimated to have affected more than 300,000 computers across 150 countries, causing billions of US dollars in damage.

North Korea’s state-led cyber operations start with the selection of young students who demonstrate outstanding academic performance, particularly in science and mathematics. These students are provided with specialised computer training at the elite Kumsong Middle School in Pyongyang.

They then advance to one of several colleges, including Mirim College, Moranbong College, Kim Il Sung University or the Kim Chaek University of Technology. In these colleges, students undergo training programmes combining military studies with advanced cyber skills.
As of 2024, North Korea was estimated to have trained roughly 8,400 state-sponsored cyber personnel through these programmes. This figure is likely to have increased since then.

North Korea’s investment in cyber personnel training is driven by clear strategic goals. The main objectives of early North Korean cyber-attacks were to create social disruption in what Pyongyang sees as hostile states.

Examples include the 2013 DarkSeoul attack and the 2014 cyber-attack on Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power. In the DarkSeoul attack, around 32,000 computers belonging to major South Korean broadcasting networks and financial institutions were disrupted by malware.

The attack on Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power involved the theft and disclosure of personal employee information, nuclear power plant blueprints and technical documents. Both attacks aimed to disrupt critical systems and generate public anxiety. They allowed North Korea to exert pressure on its adversaries without engaging in direct military confrontation.

In recent years, however, North Korea’s cyber operations have shifted towards making money. The more recent cyber operations are part of the country’s broader efforts to maintain regime stability and fund its nuclear programme following years of international sanctions.

In 2024, a UN panel of experts estimated that the money stolen in North Korean cyber-attacks generated half of North Korea’s foreign currency income. One unnamed panel member added that stolen money funds “40% of the weapons of mass destruction programmes”.

Several measures are in place to defend against North Korean cyber operations. These include financial sanctions and international efforts to disrupt money-laundering networks. Governments worldwide also work closely with the private sector to exchange intelligence, identify suspicious transactions and trace and recover stolen cryptocurrency.

But the current measures have not been sufficient to prevent attacks. A key reason for this is the fact that international investigations and enforcement remain constrained by national jurisdictions and sovereignty.

As in the physical world, one country cannot access data or conduct an investigation within another country’s territory without its consent. Digital evidence can be also be quickly deleted or altered, so reliance on international cooperation can make an effective and timely response difficult.

Preventing North Korean cyber operations completely may be unrealistic. But there are several ways to make these activities less profitable and more difficult to carry out. These include strengthening identity verification procedures to prevent North Korean IT workers from gaining employment with false identities.

They also include improving information-sharing between governments and private companies and enhancing cyber resilience. This would minimise the damage to targeted organisations and help them recover more quickly when attacks occur.
Ultimately, the goal should not only be to prevent attacks, but also to disrupt the networks that enable them, limit the financial gains and reduce their impact.

articles.title: In Kosovo, a new app makes reporting problems to the government fast and easy
articles.author: Nurbek Bekmurzaev
paras: It will cut the bureacratic red tape that plagues state institutions
Originally published on Global Voices
Image by Sbunker. Used with permission.

This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.

One of the biggest barriers for people’s effective engagement with the authorities in Kosovo is a confusing and unresponsive bureaucracy. Whenever citizens want to report a problem in their community, such as potholes or illegal waste disposal, they are met with a system that requires them to know the roles and responsibilities of various state institutions and handle necessary paperwork themselves.

When submitted to the wrong agency or without proper documents, citizens’ complaints are either ignored or can take long periods to be processed, which discourages engagement and has an adverse effect on people’s trust in the government. Ultimately, it deteriorates the already challenging situation regarding transparency, communication, and accountability of state bodies in Kosovo.

In 2026, a local non-governmental organization (NGO), Sbunker, responded to this challenge by creating an online platform called Kosovo.report to help citizens report their complaints to the authorities in a quick and easy manner. Global Voices conducted an email interview with Hana Deva, project manager at SBunker, to learn more about their initiative. The interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.
Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Sparks project.

Hana Deva (HD): Sbunker is a non-governmental organization founded in 2016, focused on providing analysis and informed perspectives on important political, economic, social, and cultural issues in Kosovo and the Western Balkans. Through our Disinfo program, we monitor local and regional media content to identify and address disinformation. Sbunker produces podcasts and other media content exploring political and social developments, philosophical, cultural, and theoretical discussions. We joined the Digital Sparks project because we wanted to create a direct form of civic engagement through technology. This led to the development of Kosovo.report, a platform designed to give citizens a simple way to report problems and submit requests concerning their neighborhoods and local communities. The platform is intended to act as a link between citizens and public institutions by helping these reports reach the relevant institutions and making the process more accessible to the citizens.
GV: What issue/challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?

HD: Through our work in media and civic engagement, we became interested in how citizens communicate everyday problems in their communities to public institutions. Research on public administration in Kosovo points to fragmented public service delivery, inconsistencies in administrative procedures and digital services, and continuing challenges in communication between citizens and institutions. This can make the process of reporting an issue to the right department unclear. Kosovo.report was developed with this challenge in mind. The idea is to give citizens a more straightforward way to report an issue, without requiring them to first determine which institution or department is responsible. Based on the type and location of the problem, the platform is designed to route the report to the appropriate department and allow the citizen to follow what happens afterwards.
GV: What are the key changes/activities that your organization implemented during your participation in the project?

HD: Our main work has been the development of Kosovo.report, from the initial concept to a functional platform now being prepared for its pilot phase. Alongside this development, we have coordinated with the Municipality of Prishtina to determine how reports should reach the appropriate departments, and prepared a Memorandum of Understanding to formalise this cooperation. Beyond the platform, Sbunker has served as a capacity hub for other Digital Sparks project grantees during the project period. We organized meetings and an advocacy workshop where grantees worked on developing a joint advocacy event. We also hosted a young fellow, Bora Dibra, from the Albanian organization IRSH (Young Intellectuals, Hope), for a one-month fellowship focused on digital civic engagement, media literacy, and participatory advocacy.
GV: How did your participation in the project impact your organization’s beneficiaries and the community that you serve? Please provide examples.

HD: The project has allowed Sbunker to expand the way we approach civic engagement. Much of our work traditionally focused on informing citizens and creating public debate through publications. Through Kosovo.report, we are developing a tool that takes this a step further by giving citizens a channel through which they can raise problems in their communities and have their reports directed to the relevant departments. The next step will be the pilot of Kosovo.report in the capital, Prishtina, where we will be able to test the platform with citizens, gather their feedback, and identify what needs to be improved.
GV: How has your own knowledge, awareness, and experience with digital democracy and civic space changed, thanks to your participation in the project?

HD: Developing Kosovo.report has given us experience in creating a digital tool through which citizens can report issues and direct them to the relevant departments. The process has also involved working with the Municipality of Prishtina as we prepare for the pilot phase of the project, which is a different scope of work from Sbunker's focus on media and public debate. Our role as a capacity hub has also given us an opportunity to work more closely with individual grantees and other civil society organizations, learn about their projects in digital democracy, and the challenges in their communities. Taken together, these activities have expanded Sbunker’s experience from media, analysis and public debate, to developing digital tools and working more closely with civil society organizations and public institutions.
GV: What are the most valuable lessons and experiences you are taking away from this project?

HD: One of the most valuable experiences has been developing something that is intended to have a direct use in people’s everyday lives. With Kosovo.report, we are taking a different approach by developing a platform that citizens can use in their communities and communicate with relevant institutions. Building the platform has also given us a better sense of what it takes to turn an idea for civic participation into something that works in practice. The capacity hub and fellowship have added to this experience by allowing us to work with people approaching digital democracy and civic engagement from different projects and contexts.
GV: What comes next? How will you apply the learning and digital capacity you have built in your future work and within your community?

HD: For us, Kosovo.report is a starting point for what we want to do in the digital democracy area. The current focus is on Prishtina, but we want to take the platform beyond the pilot and explore opportunities to connect with other municipalities and public institutions across Kosovo. The first phase is helping us see what works, what needs to be improved, and how the platform can better respond to the needs of local communities. The project has also strengthened Sbunker’s capacity to develop digital approaches to civic participation. We want to build on that experience in our future work by looking more closely at the needs of the communities we work with and explore where digital tools can help address them. We also want to continue the relationships developed through this project, both with civil society organizations and collaborators, and see where they can lead beyond the project.
